He answers four things: but because he had not perceived the force of the argument, he improvises (ἀποσχεδιάζει). The Apostle said that death pervaded into all men: the cause without doubt is because all sinned. But which sin ought to be understood is the question. Some want habitual sin inhering in all to be understood; others Adam's actual sin imputed to all in the order of nature before they are vicious. Habitual inhering sin propagated from Adam into all is a certain cause — that is, confessed by all the orthodox. For concerning that vice — that it exists and is a cause of death, being truly sin and truly making us liable to death — there is no controversy among us. That is confirmed by the common confession of faith in the clearest and most express words. But concerning Adam's actual sin — whether it is imputed before corruption, and whether that imputation is the cause why death has pervaded into all — the matter is not certain and liquid: for that is what is now controverted among us. Again, the vice inhering in each of us is a nearer cause of our death than Adam's first actual sin which is said to be imputed to us — not only earlier in the order of nature than we were corrupted, but even by some thousands of years before we began to be and to live. Therefore when those two causes are compared with each other, that is certain because not controverted, this uncertain because controverted; that is proximate in the same subject with its effect — that is, with death — this remote because in another subject, from us not only by the order of generating nature but also by time very remote, and between which and death a nearer cause is interposed, namely corruption. Now, I think, Reader, you yourself understand through yourself the learned man's aberrant responses. For since it is certain and in no way controverted among us that there inheres in all a sin that merits death and on account of which all die, why concerning that sin do we not take the Apostle's words in which the cause of the death of all men is contained — "all sinned"? Why, that sin being set aside as if it were none, do we flee to another imputed sin, which both is controverted and is remoter from that effect — especially when the Apostle's words and the situ of the words resist?

source_text: Praeter aberrationem ab argumento sunt alia vitia in responsionibus tribus D. G. quae paucis indicabo. 1. Nos, inquit, pertendimus certam fuisse causam, quare de imputatione illa loqueretur Apostolus. Nam cum dixisset, unius hominis peccato mortem fuisse introductam in mundum, quaeri potuit, unde ea vis illi peccato, ut tantum mali non in unum aut alterum, sed in omnes invexerit: Respondet Paulus, illud inde factum, quod uno illo peccato omnes rei facti sint, sive quod uno illo peccante omnes in illo et cum illo peccavisse intelligendi sunt. Haec responsio, praeter quam quod non tangit nervum argumenti, Apostolum facit nugantem, et mutatis tantum verbis idipsum quod quaerebatur respondentem, ac pro causa effectus ipsum effectum, cujus causa quaerebatur, afferentem. Quid enim est hujus responsionis autori, peccatum in mundum introiisse? nihil, nisi peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse. Id patet clarissime ex hoc ipso ejus cap. 8. §. 8. p. 217. et aliis aliquot locis. Quid rursus ei est in Adamo omnes peccavisse? id sane, inquit, melius exponi non potest, quam si dicamus peccatum Adae omnibus imputari. eodem cap. §. 10. p. 222. Quaerenti ergo cur peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputetur ad mortem, Responderit Apostolus, quia omnibus imputatur. Quaerenti, unde ea vis illi peccato, ut imputetur non uni aut alteri, sed omnibus, respondet illud inde factum, quod illud imputetur omnibus. Quid est nugari, si hoc non est?
english: Besides the aberration from the argument there are other vices in the three responses of D. Garissoles, which I will point out in a few words. 1. "We," he says, "contend that there was a certain cause why the Apostle should speak of that imputation. For when he had said that by one man's sin death was brought into the world (Romans 5:12), it could be asked whence that force to that sin, that it brought so great an evil not upon one or another but upon all: Paul answers that it came about thence, that by that one sin all were made liable, or that that one sinning, all are to be understood to have sinned in him and with him." This response, besides that it does not touch the nerve of the argument, makes the Apostle trifling: with only the words changed he answers the very thing that was being asked, and brings forward as the cause of the effect the effect itself whose cause was being sought. For what is it, to the author of this response, that sin entered into the world? nothing, except that actual sin was imputed to all men. That is clearest from this very chapter 8, §. 8, p. 217 of his, and from some other places. What again is it to him that all sinned in Adam? that, he says, can certainly not be better expounded than if we say that Adam's sin is imputed to all — the same chapter, §. 10, p. 222. To one asking, therefore, why Adam's actual sin is imputed to all unto death, the Apostle will have answered: because it is imputed to all. To one asking whence that force to that sin, that it is imputed not to one or another but to all, he answers that it came about thence, that it is imputed to all. What is it to trifle, if this is not?

source_text: Ad duo ista vitia accedit etiam tertium. Sibi enim ipse repugnat. Nam si ea fuit mens Apostoli quam ei tribuit haec responsio, certe verba ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον construi debent, post antecedentia omnia, peccatum in mundum introiit, et per peccatum mors, et ita mors in omnes pervasit: responsio enim essent ad quaestionem, quae ex verbis illis immediate praecedentibus exoriri poterat. Id quod versionem in quo evertit. Ea enim posita construi debent verba in quo omnes peccaverunt, ante illa omnia: cohaerent enim immediate cum nomine ἀνθρώπου et est trajectio. Sic ergo construi deberent, Sicut per unum hominem, in quo omnes peccaverunt, peccatum in mundum introiit, et per peccatum mors, et ita in omnes homines mors pervasit.
english: To those two vices a third also is added. For he contradicts himself. For if that was the mind of the Apostle which this response attributes to him, certainly the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (Romans 5:12) ought to be construed after all the antecedents — "sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all" — for they would answer the question that could arise from those immediately preceding words. That overturns the version "in which." For with that version posited, the words "in which all sinned" ought to be construed before all those: for they cohere immediately with the noun ἀνθρώπου, and there is a transposition. So they ought to be construed: "As through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all men" (Romans 5:12).

source_text: Secunda similiter responsio peccat ignoratione argumenti, causamque incertam aliter quam debuit accipit, et praeterea nonnulla habet minus recte dicta. Quis dixerit, inquit, incertam causam a Paulo proponi cum I. Cor. xv. 22. ad Adamum usque protoplastam conscendit, et nos omnes dicit in Adamo mori? Quorsum hoc spectat? Ibine causam aliquam affert Apostolus, cur omnes vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo moriantur? aut suntne illa verba, in Adamo omnes moriuntur, etiam imputative, ut loquuntur, intelligenda? Deteriora sunt quae sequuntur. Nimirum, inquit, neque ibi, neque hic Apostolus proprie ad causas particulares respicit, quae residere possunt in unoquoque individuo generis humani, et propter quas fit ut moriantur: sed causam generalem exponit quae omnes in genere ex aequo respiciat etc. Perinde loquitur, quasi corruptio haereditaria non esset causa generalis omnes homines ex aequo respiciens: Cum illa tamen tam sit communis, quam communis est eorum qui peccaverunt mors, quam communis est illis natura humana, immo quam communis dicitur esse imputatio. Ita paulatim doctrina de corruptionis haereditariae vi et reatu, quam summo studio primi reformatores tuebantur, negligitur ac prope obliteratur, ut det locum illi imputationi, quam magni illi viri, aut ignorarunt prorsus, aut etiam refutarunt.
english: The second response likewise sins by ignorance of the argument, and takes the uncertain cause otherwise than it ought, and besides has some things less rightly said. "Who will have said," he says, "that an uncertain cause is proposed by Paul, when in 1 Corinthians 15:22 he ascends as far as Adam the first-formed, and says that we all die in Adam?" What is the point of this? Does the Apostle there bring forward some cause why all die by the force of the communion they have with Adam? Or are those words, "in Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22), to be understood even imputatively, as they speak? Worse are the things that follow. "Namely," he says, "neither there nor here does the Apostle properly look to particular causes that can reside in each individual of the human race and on account of which it comes about that they die; but he sets out a general cause that looks upon all in the genus equally," and so on. He speaks just as if hereditary corruption were not a general cause looking upon all men equally — when yet that is as common as the death of those who have sinned is common, as human nature is common to them, indeed as imputation is said to be common. So little by little the doctrine of the force and guilt of hereditary corruption, which the first reformers defended with highest zeal, is neglected and nearly blotted out, that it may give place to that imputation which those great men either altogether did not know, or even refuted.

source_text: Neque par est, addit, ut eam causam dicamus esse remotam et longinquam, quia hic non ad annorum et saeculorum spatia, sed ad rei efficacitatem respiciendum est. Quid? an injustitia, quae in me non haesit, sed in solo Adamo, tot annorum millibus antequam essem mortuo, causa est aeque immediata ac proxima mihi vel morti meae, ac illa quae in me haeret intime, et est omnium confessione mortis meae causa? Annon etiam peccatum Adami secuta est corruptio, et hanc mors? est igitur corruptio causa propinquior mortis quam peccatum quod in solo haesit Adamo. Neque vero, subjungit, qui corruptionem ab Adamo derivari dicunt, Adamum ideo proponunt, tanquam causam remotam et distantem corruptionis illius, nimirum, quia est nobis cum eo ratione sanguinis proxima unio, etsi non ratione personae. Immo eum proponunt, tanquam causam corruptionis illius remotam et distantem, hoc est, primam, unde ad alios omnes dimanavit. Itaque quod sanguis hic a persona distinguitur, et illius, non hujus, ratione nobis esse dicitur proxima cum Adamo unio, id equidem non intelligo. Tam enim sanguis meus a sanguine, et natura mea a natura, quam persona a persona Adami differt: differentia est utriusque pariter numerica, non specifica: Et quam personam meam, tam naturam etiam meam per omnes meos intermedios parentes ab Adamo traxi. Est enim Adamus pater noster non proximus, sed primus; nihilque ab eo nisi per proximos meos parentes, accepi, aut accipere potui.
english: "Nor is it fair," he adds, "that we should say that cause is remote and far off, because here one must look not to spaces of years and ages, but to the efficacy of the thing." What? is an injustice that did not stick in me, but in Adam alone, dead some thousands of years before I existed, a cause equally immediate and proximate to me or to my death, as that which inheres in me most inwardly and is by the confession of all the cause of my death? Did not corruption also follow Adam's sin, and death this? corruption is therefore a nearer cause of death than the sin that stuck in Adam alone. "Nor indeed," he subjoins, "do those who say corruption is derived from Adam propose Adam on that account as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — namely, because there is for us with him a most near union by reason of blood, though not by reason of person." On the contrary they propose him as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — that is, the first, from which it flowed out to all others. Therefore that blood is here distinguished from person, and that by reason of the former, not of the latter, a most near union with Adam is said to be ours — that for my part I do not understand. For my blood differs from blood, and my nature from nature, as much as person from Adam's person: the difference of each alike is numerical, not specific. And as I drew my person, so also my nature, through all my intermediate parents from Adam. For Adam is our father not nearest but first; and I have received, or could receive, nothing from him except through my nearest parents.

source_text: Sed, inquit, cum hic instituatur inter Christum et Adamum comparatio, non magis dicendum est inobedientiam ab Adamo commissam, esse causam remotam nostrae condemnationis, quam obedientiam a Christo praestitam, esse causam remotam nostrae justificationis. Quasi vero non possit comparatio inter duas causas effectuum oppositorum institui, cum sunt in suo genere primae, nisi utraque sit pariter proxima! Quis nescit obedientiam Christi esse justificationis nostrae causam adaequatam et unicam, inobedientiam vero Adami condemnationis nostrae nonnisi inadaequatam et partialem? damnamur enim non ob solum peccatum actuale Adami, sed etiam ob inhaerentem nobis corruptionem haereditariam, et alia omnia nostra peccata sive actualia sive habitualia; cum tamen ob unam Christi obedientiam, nullo autem modo ob nostram, justificemur. Haec igitur, cum sola et unica justificationis causa sit, eadem et prima et proxima est; illa vero cum non sola sit, sed una cum ea aliae multae sint causae condemnationis, ita prima est, ut nihil necesse sit proximam esse. Quid? nonne peccatum et per peccatum condemnationem trahimus ab Adamo propagatione naturali? Nonne et Patres olim, et primi nostri Reformatores imitationi Pelagianae opponere solebant propagationem peccati, nulla imputationis facta mentione? Atqui propagationis naturalis, in suo quidem genere, prima est causa Adamus, sed cujusque nostrum proxima aut immediata profecto non est. Hic ergo maximum cernitur Adamum inter et Christum discrimen. Adamus est generationis nostrae causa remotissima, cum regenerationis nostrae Christus sit causa proxima. Filii sumus Adami non proximi sed remoti: inter nos enim et Adamum alii multi interjecti sunt; Filii vero Christi proximi sumus, quotquot in eum credimus. Per fidem enim unimur Christo recta et immediate, necnon per ejus Spiritum, qui cum unus tantum numero sit et in Christo et in omnibus nobis, nos Christo tam immediate copulat, ut inter Christum et fidelem intermedius nemo sit. Haec cum non ignoraret Vir Doctus, qui potuit sic loqui? Denique in causis meritoriis, inquit, quales sunt de quibus agimus, semper est proximitas, quia meritum illud semper ἐγγύς et efficaciter agit. Egregium argumentum! quasi non possit pariter efficacia, ac causa, distingui in remotam et proximam! sua enim cuique causae vis et, cum sequitur effectum, efficacia est; alioqui non esset causa. Annon Adamus efficaciter naturam suam et corruptionem in nos propagavit? Attamen naturae et corruptionis nostrae causa non est nisi remota. Non est autem ipse causa meritoria condemnationis nostrae, sed hujus causa causae; manavit enim ab eo corruptio haereditaria nostrae condemnationis causa proxima seu immediata, hujus autem causa fuit peccatum actuale Adami. Possumusne similiter dicere, obedientiam Christi causam fuisse alicujus virtutis vel obedientiae, quae sit causa justificationis nostrae? Eatenus igitur inter Christi obedientiam et Adami inobedientiam discrimen est memorabile, et illa proxima justificationis, haec remota condemnationis nostrae (corruptio enim interponitur) causa dicenda est. Alioqui quomodo peccatum actuale Adami causa esse posset condemnationis nostrae meritoria et proxima? Primum si non est nostrum nisi per imputationem, non meretur condemnationem nostram nisi imputationis interventu. Non est igitur causa meritoria nostrae condemnationis per se, sed per accidens tantum, ratione illius imputationis, quae est actio divina, atque adeo supernaturalis et voluntaria: cum tamen obedientia Christi sit causa meritoria justificationis nostrae per se; quippe, eo fine ac consilio a vade nostro loco nostro praestita. Quo posito sequitur, quod sumus peccatores et condemnamur, id esse divinae illi actioni per se ascribendum, peccato vero Adami nonnisi per accidens, id quod ut credam vel faciam adduci me mea nullo modo patitur conscientia. Deinde qui imputat alicui homini peccatum, supponit illum hominem esse, qui damnat ad mortem supponit eum quem damnat vivere. Cum ergo nostri esse et vivere, quod natura condemnationem nostram antecedit, non sit Adamus causa nisi remota, qui potest esse condemnationis nostrae causa proxima?
english: "But," he says, "since a comparison is here instituted between Christ and Adam, the disobedience committed by Adam is no more to be called a remote cause of our condemnation than the obedience performed by Christ is to be called a remote cause of our justification." As if a comparison could not be instituted between two causes of opposite effects, when they are first in their kind, unless each alike is proximate! Who does not know that Christ's obedience is the adequate and only cause of our justification, but Adam's disobedience only an inadequate and partial cause of our condemnation? for we are condemned not on account of Adam's actual sin alone, but also on account of the hereditary corruption inhering in us, and all our other sins whether actual or habitual; whereas yet we are justified on account of Christ's one obedience, and in no way on account of ours. This cause, therefore, since it is the sole and only cause of justification, is the same both first and proximate; but that, since it is not alone, but together with it there are many other causes of condemnation, is first in such a way that there is no necessity that it be proximate. What? do we not draw sin and, through sin, condemnation from Adam by natural propagation? Did not both the Fathers of old and our first Reformers use to oppose the propagation of sin to Pelagian imitation, with no mention made of imputation? And yet of natural propagation, in its own kind indeed, Adam is the first cause, but of each of us the nearest or immediate cause he certainly is not. Here therefore the greatest difference is seen between Adam and Christ. Adam is the most remote cause of our generation, whereas Christ is the proximate cause of our regeneration. We are sons of Adam not nearest but remote: for between us and Adam many others are interposed; but we are nearest sons of Christ, as many as believe in him. For by faith we are united to Christ straight and immediately, and also by his Spirit, who, since he is only one in number both in Christ and in all of us, couples us to Christ so immediately that between Christ and the believer there is no middle person. Since the learned man was not ignorant of these things, how could he speak so? "Finally in meritorious causes," he says, "of the kind we are dealing with, there is always proximity, because that merit always acts near (ἐγγύς) and efficaciously." A fine argument! as if efficacy, like cause, could not equally be distinguished into remote and proximate! for each cause has its own force, and when the effect follows, that is efficacy; otherwise it would not be a cause. Did not Adam efficaciously propagate his nature and corruption into us? And yet he is only a remote cause of our nature and corruption. But he himself is not the meritorious cause of our condemnation, but the cause of this cause; for from him flowed the hereditary corruption that is the proximate or immediate cause of our condemnation, and of this the cause was Adam's actual sin. Can we likewise say that Christ's obedience was the cause of some virtue or obedience that is the cause of our justification? To that extent, therefore, there is a memorable difference between Christ's obedience and Adam's disobedience, and the former is to be called the proximate cause of justification, the latter the remote cause of our condemnation (for corruption is interposed). Otherwise how could Adam's actual sin be a meritorious and proximate cause of our condemnation? First, if it is not ours except by imputation, it does not merit our condemnation except by the intervention of imputation. It is therefore not a meritorious cause of our condemnation through itself, but only through an accident, by reason of that imputation, which is a divine action, and so supernatural and voluntary: whereas yet Christ's obedience is a meritorious cause of our justification through itself; namely, performed to that end and counsel by our surety in our place. That granted, it follows that our being sinners and being condemned is to be ascribed through itself to that divine action, but to Adam's sin only through an accident — which my conscience will in no way let me be led to believe or do. Next, he who imputes sin to some man presupposes that that man exists; he who condemns to death presupposes that he whom he condemns lives. Since therefore of our existing and living, which by nature precedes our condemnation, Adam is only a remote cause, how can he be the proximate cause of our condemnation?

source_text: Sequitur ratio quarta. Scopus Apostoli non patitur ut ita vertantur; coepit enim Apostolus vers. 12. comparationem inter Christum & Adamum instituere eo modo, ut affirmaret per unum hominem peccatum introiisse, & per peccatum mortem, adeo ut mors in omnes homines pervagata sit. Quia vero mirum videri potuit, tantam fuisse in unius hominis uno peccato vim atque efficacitatem, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, ne quis indigne quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, addit, id mirum videri non debere, cum omnes peccaverint. Ut igitur Adam in mortem incidit, quia peccavit; sic & omnes pariter in mortem incidunt, quia omnes peccaverunt.
english: The fourth reason follows. The Apostle's scope will not allow them to be turned that way; for the Apostle began at verse 12 (Romans 5:12) to institute a comparison between Christ and Adam in such a manner as to affirm that through one man sin entered, and through sin death, so that death spread abroad upon all men. But because it could seem strange that there was so great force and efficacy in one man's one sin that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death, lest anyone should suspect anything unworthy of God, he adds that this ought not to seem strange, since all have sinned. As therefore Adam fell into death because he sinned, so also all alike fall into death because all have sinned.

source_text: Quid reponit vir doctus? Primo, inquit, notetur respondentis confessio: Nam dum agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per unum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse unum unius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum, eadem ratione omnia illa argumenta confutat & convellit, quibus supra moliebatur alius confirmare, hic peccati nomine non ipsius Adami peccatum, sed nostram internam & originalem corruptionem tantum intelligendam esse. Ita-ne, omnia illa argumenta confutat & convellit? Possunt-ne unius simplici affirmatione, alterius argumenta & multa, & valida, & diu post illam affirmationem excogitata & proposita confutari & convelli? Si est ita, nullum est argumentum usque adeo necessarium, & demonstrativum, quod non possit ea ratione facillime confutari & convelli. Argumenta autem illa, quia sunt posterioris manuscripti, quam sint valida & invicta, tum fiet manifestum, cum instituetur manuscripti illius cum libro D. Gar. comparatio.
english: What does the learned man reply? "First," he says, "let the respondent's confession be noted: for while he acknowledges that that sin which is said to have entered through one man is one sin of one man, namely Adam's, by the same reason he confutes and overthrows all those arguments by which another above was striving to confirm that here by the name of sin not Adam's own sin, but only our inward and original corruption, is to be understood." Does he so confute and overthrow all those arguments? Can another's arguments — many, and strong, and long after that affirmation devised and proposed — be confuted and overthrown by one man's simple affirmation? If it is so, there is no argument so necessary and demonstrative that it cannot by that reason be most easily confuted and overthrown. But those arguments, because they belong to a later manuscript, how valid and invincible they are will then become plain when a comparison of that manuscript with Doctor Garissoles's book is instituted.

source_text: Quid vero dices, candide Lector, si id non confitetur doctissimus autor illius rationis, quod hic confiteri dicitur? Certe non agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per unum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse unum unius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum: id non sentit: id neque totidem verbis dixit, neque aequipollentibus. Dixit tantum in uno unius peccato tantam fuisse vim, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret: sed non dixit illud unum unius peccatum idem numero in omnes homines ingressum esse, & proxime mortem invexisse. Nempe peccatum quod introiit in mundum est unius peccati unius hominis effectum, & per unum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum & mors vi unius peccati, quod sese propagatione naturali diffudit, & multiplicavit, & cum natura humana, cui inhaeret, propagavit. Itaque totam hominum multitudinem morti addixit sui in omnes homines propagatione, ac secundum numerum multiplicatione. Haec est praestantissimi illius viri mens, neque sibi, neque Placeo contradicentis.
english: But what will you say, candid reader, if the most learned author of that reason does not confess what he is here said to confess? Certainly he does not acknowledge that that sin which is said to have entered through one man is one sin of one man, namely Adam's: he does not hold that; he said it neither in so many words nor in equivalent ones. He said only that in one man's one sin there was such force that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death; but he did not say that that one sin of one man entered into all men as the same in number, and brought death in immediately. Namely, the sin that entered into the world is the effect of one sin of one man; and through one man sin entered into the world, and death by the force of one sin, which diffused and multiplied itself by natural propagation, and propagated with the human nature in which it inheres. Therefore it sentenced the whole multitude of men to death by its propagation into all men, and by multiplication according to number. This is that most excellent man's mind, contradicting neither himself nor Placeus.

source_text: Haec prima fuit D. G. responsio. 2. Ad dubium, inquit, quod emergere potuit in lectorum animis, nulla esset plane Apostoli responsio legitima, si talem daret, qualem vult Vir Doctus. Dubium enim hoc est, quomodo tanta sit vis in uno unius Adami peccato, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addicat. Responsio dicitur esse, id inde fieri, quod omnes peccaverint in sua propria persona. Hoc vero ludere est, non dubio satisfacere. Nam haec quidem ratio esse potest, propter quam morti omnes addicantur, quia omnes peccarunt. Sed hic non quaeritur, quare omnes morti addicantur, verum hoc potius, cur in uno unius Adami peccato tanta vis sit, ut hunc effectum producat, nempe mortem. Responsio igitur debet agere de peccato illo Adami, non de nostro uniuscujusque, de quo nihil dictum fuerat in dubio proposito. Itaque ut apposita sit responsio, necessarium est, ut illud ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, interpretemur de peccato ipsius Adami, quod omnes morti addicat, propterea quod ejus reatus in omnes descendit, sive quia propter imputationem commune sit omnibus. Hoc ita clarum est & evidens, ut hic oporteat valde festinasse disputatorem. Festinavit quidem fortasse autor hujus rationis, sed non nimis: optime enim disputat. Sed an festinaverit D. G. nescio, illud certe mihi constat, eum hic, ut alibi passim, haud recte disputare.
english: This was Doctor Garissoles's first response. 2. "As to the doubt," he says, "which could arise in readers' minds, there would plainly be no legitimate response of the Apostle if he gave such a one as the learned man wants. For this is the doubt: how there is so great force in one sin of one Adam that it sentences the whole multitude of men to death. The response is said to be that this comes about thence, that all have sinned in their own person. But this is to play, not to satisfy the doubt. For this reason can indeed be why all are sentenced to death, because all have sinned. But here it is not asked why all are sentenced to death, but rather this: why in one sin of one Adam there is so great force that it produces this effect, namely death. The response therefore ought to deal with that sin of Adam, not with each of ours, about which nothing had been said in the doubt proposed. Therefore, for the response to be fitting, it is necessary that we interpret ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον of Adam's own sin, which sentences all to death because its reatus descends upon all, or because through imputation it becomes common to all. This is so clear and evident that here the disputant must have been in a great hurry." The author of this reason may perhaps have hurried, but not too much: for he disputes excellently. But whether Doctor Garissoles hurried, I do not know; this much is certain to me, that he here, as elsewhere throughout, does not dispute rightly.

source_text: Non ludit, sed revera dubio satisfacit Responsio. Duobus enim modis in unius hominis uno peccato tantam vim fuisse, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, intelligi poterat, uno, si ponatur, quod facit hoc loco D. G. Deum toti hominum multitudini unum illud unius hominis peccatum immediate imputasse, atque ob illud imputatum eam morti addixisse. Altero, si intelligatur, peccatum illud sese naturali quodam contagio, ab uno homine in alios omnes propagasse & multiplicasse, atque ita, quoniam omnes peccaverunt, morti addictos fuisse. Apostolus ne Lector priorem modum cogitans, indigne quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, posteriorem docet, affirmans omnes homines morti fuisse addictos, non quia unus tantum peccavit, sed quia omnes peccaverunt; non proxime ob unius unum peccatum, sed ob suum quisque sibi insitum, ab illo uno propagatum, quae propagatio vocibus ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ita, non minus ad peccatum quam ad mortem pertinentibus, satis innuitur. Audi, quaeso humanissime Lector, Calvinum, a cujus doctrina recedant necesse est qui nos innovatae doctrinae accusant, Comm. in Rom. 5. 12. Observa quem hic ponat ordinem. Peccatum enim praecessisse dicit: ex eo sequutam esse mortem. Sunt enim qui contendunt, nos ita peccato Adae esse perditos ac si nulla nostra culpa periremus, ideo tantum quasi ille nobis peccasset. (Vix potuit clarius imputatio antecedens describi, quam sequi putantur mors animae, id est, corruptio haereditaria, & mors corporis ac aeterna, tanquam poenae proprie dictae.) Atqui diserte affirmat Paulus, in omnes propagatum esse peccatum, qui ejus poenam luunt. Atque id deinde propius urget, quum rationem assignat paulo post, cur omnis Adae posteritas subjaceat mortis imperio. Nempe, inquit, quoniam omnes peccavimus. Porro istud peccare, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Illa enim naturalis pravitas quam e matris utero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram Domino, & ejus ultionem meretur. Atque hoc est peccatum quod vocant Originale. Et paulo post, Peccavimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti sumus. Et iterum, Sequitur ergo pravitatem nobis ingenitam, & haereditariam notari. Nihil potuit dici clarius & disertius. Gratulatur sibi Placeus cum videt per latus suum peti Calvinum, seque cum eo pariter oppugnari, & desertae antiquae doctrinae, aut potius eam deserantium vices luget. Notetur hic rursus nova, &, ut mihi quidem videtur, Deo injuriosa doctrina, peccatum Adami propter imputationem commune fieri omnibus. Quod igitur commune est omnibus id non vi aut contagio aut naturali propagationi illius peccati ascribendum est, sed Deo, cui libuit imputando facere omnibus commune, quod alioqui commune non fuisset. Unde igitur nostra perditio, nisi ex Deo, qui nos fecit peccatores alienum peccatum efficiendo nostrum? Et cur peccatum illud nobis imputavit, & fecit nostrum, nosque peccatores? Nulla causa affertur, aut afferri potest, nisi quia ita ei libuit. Non excitatur conscientia tua, pie Lector? non refugit talem doctrinam? non exhorrescit? Sed pergamus.
english: The response does not play, but truly satisfies the doubt. For in two ways it could be understood that there was such force in one man's one sin that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death: in one way, if it is supposed — which Doctor Garissoles does in this place — that God immediately imputed that one sin of one man to the whole multitude of men, and for that imputed sin sentenced it to death. In the other, if it is understood that that sin propagated and multiplied itself by a certain natural contagion from one man into all others, and so, since all have sinned, they were sentenced to death. The Apostle, lest the reader thinking the former way should suspect anything unworthy of God, teaches the latter, affirming that all men were sentenced to death not because one alone sinned, but because all have sinned; not immediately on account of one man's one sin, but on account of each man's own implanted in him, propagated from that one — which propagation is sufficiently hinted by the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, pertaining no less to sin than to death. Hear, I ask, most kindly reader, Calvin, from whose doctrine those who accuse us of innovated doctrine must of necessity withdraw — Commentary on Romans 5:12. Observe what order he sets here. For he says that sin preceded: from it death followed. For there are those who contend that we are so lost by Adam's sin as if we perished by no fault of our own, only because he had as it were sinned for us. (Antecedent imputation could scarcely be described more clearly than as that which death of the soul — that is, hereditary corruption — and death of the body and eternal death are thought to follow, as punishments properly so called.) And yet Paul expressly affirms that sin has been propagated to all who undergo its punishment. And then he presses that more closely when a little later he assigns the reason why all Adam's posterity lies under the empire of death. Namely, he says, because we have all sinned. Further, that 'to sin' is to be corrupted and spoiled. For that natural depravity which we bring from the mother's womb, even if it does not so quickly put forth its fruits, is yet sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And this is the sin which they call Original. And a little later: We have therefore all sinned, because we are all imbued with natural corruption. And again: It follows therefore that depravity inborn and hereditary in us is marked. Nothing could be said more clearly and expressly. Placeus congratulates himself when he sees Calvin struck through his side, and himself attacked together with him, and mourns the lot of the deserted ancient doctrine, or rather of those deserting it. Let it be noted here again the new doctrine — and, as it seems to me, injurious to God — that Adam's sin becomes common to all because of imputation. What therefore is common to all is to be ascribed not to the force or contagion or natural propagation of that sin, but to God, to whom it pleased by imputing to make common to all what otherwise would not have been common. Whence then our perdition, if not from God, who made us sinners by making another's sin ours? And why did he impute that sin to us, and make it ours, and us sinners? No cause is brought, or can be brought, except that it so pleased him. Is your conscience not stirred, pious reader? Does it not shrink from such a doctrine? Does it not shudder? But let us go on.

source_text: Quinta & ultima ratio his verbis concepta est § XI. pag. 224. Ea interpretatio confirmatur vers. 13. sequenti, qui per particulam γάρ connectitur cum precedenti. Dubitare enim aliquis potuit, an omnes homines revera peccaverint; Id igitur Apostolus probat eo argumento, quod ubicunque mors est, ibi necesse est esse peccatum. Mors autem non extitit modo, sed & regnavit in omnes illos qui vixerunt iis temporibus, quae inter primum peccatum Adami & legem interfluxerunt: omnes illi ergo fuerunt peccato obnoxii. Respondeo inquit D. G. Abfit vero ut ejusmodi analysim accipiamus, quae ex divino Apostolo facit ineptum circulatorem. [§ XVIII.] Bona verba: ineptum circulatorem! Abfit a nobis tam grande crimen. Quomodo vero id probat? Nam, inquit, Apostolus versu 12. probat omnes esse addictos morti, quia peccaverunt, postea vers. 13. probat omnes peccasse, quia morti addicti sunt, & mors in omnes regnat. Hoc scilicet est esse ineptum circulatorem.
english: The fifth and last reason is framed in these words (§ XI, p. 224): "That interpretation is confirmed by the following verse 13, which is joined to the preceding by the particle γάρ. For someone might doubt whether all men have truly sinned; the Apostle therefore proves it by this argument, that wherever death is, there sin must necessarily be. But death not only existed, but also reigned over all those who lived in the times that flowed between Adam's first sin and the law: all those, therefore, were liable to sin." "I answer," says Doctor Garissoles, "far be it that we should accept such an analysis, which makes of the divine Apostle an inept circular arguer" (§ XVIII). Fine words: an inept circular arguer! Far be so great a crime from us. But how does he prove it? "For," he says, "the Apostle in verse 12 proves that all are sentenced to death because they have sinned; afterward in verse 13 he proves that all have sinned because they are sentenced to death, and death reigns over all. This, of course, is to be an inept circular arguer."

source_text: Atqui non dixit illius rationis eruditissimus autor, Apostolum versu 12. probare, omnes esse addictos morti? Relege quaeso & considera rationem, quemadmodum ab ipso Garissolio recitata fuerat § XI. & a me exscripta. Num tale quid in ea animadvertis? aut ex ea bona consequentia deduci potest? Eccur vero Apostolus id probare instituisset, quod Scriptura, & omnium seculorum experientia, genusque adeo humanum universum perpetuo confitetur & clamat? Ecquis etiam credat, Apostolum probare voluisse clarius per obscurius? Clarius enim est omnes mori, quam omnes peccasse. Non igitur probat, sed ne viderentur omnes homines ob unicum unius hominis peccatum eis imputatum mori, affirmat per unum hominem ita mortem ingressam esse in genus humanum, ut non sola in omnes homines invaserit, sed ejus etiam causa, peccatum. Itaque mori omnes non proxime ob unum illud actuale unius hominis peccatum, sed ob suum quemque sibi insitum, ab illo derivatum. Fingit ergo D. G. probationem circularem ubi nulla est.
english: And yet the most learned author of that reason did not say that the Apostle in verse 12 is proving that all are sentenced to death. Reread, I ask, and consider the reason as it had been recited by Garissoles himself at § XI and copied out by me. Do you notice anything of the kind in it? Or can a sound consequence be drawn from it? Why indeed would the Apostle have set about proving what Scripture, and the experience of every age, and the whole human race besides, forever confess and cry aloud? Who also would believe that the Apostle meant to prove the clearer by the obscurer? For that all die is clearer than that all have sinned. He does not, therefore, prove; but lest all men should seem to die on account of one man's one sin imputed to them, he affirms that through one man death so entered the human race that not death alone invaded all men, but also its cause — sin. And so all die not immediately on account of that one actual sin of one man, but on account of each man's own implanted in him, derived from that one. Doctor Garissoles therefore invents a circular proof where there is none.

source_text: quanquam si esset, non tam circulus a Philosophis damnatus, quam regressus ab iisdem laudatus dici deberet: constaret enim ex duabus demonstrationibus, altera τὸ ὅτι, altera τὸ διότι, illa pariente distinctam effectus, hac confusam causae notitiam. Eandem autem circulationem cum ipse sibi objecisset D. G. expedire sese ex ea non potuit. Posteriorem enim tantum rationem attigit, priorem, ex qua pendebat circulus, alto involvit silentio. Peto igitur ex ejus mente, num Apostolus probet vs. 12. omnes esse morti addictos, quia peccatum Adae ipsis imputatur? Si ais, manet circularis argumentatio: statim enim vs. 13. & 14. probabit omnibus peccatum Adae imputari, quia omnes sunt morti addicti. Si negas, tollis quidem circulum; sed neque id negavit D. G. neque ut se ex eo circulo educeret, quicquam ejusmodi tentavit: fecit ergo id, cujus nos falso accusabat, ex Apostolo divino ineptum, ut loquitur, circulatorem.
english: And yet if there were one, it ought to be called not so much a circle condemned by the philosophers as a regress praised by the same: for it would consist of two demonstrations, one τὸ ὅτι, the other τὸ διότι — the former producing a distinct knowledge of the effect, the latter a confused knowledge of the cause. But when Doctor Garissoles had objected this same circularity to himself, he could not extricate himself from it. For he touched only the later reason; the prior one, on which the circle hung, he wrapped in deep silence. I ask, therefore, from his mind: does the Apostle in verse 12 prove that all are sentenced to death because Adam's sin is imputed to them? If you say yes, the circular argumentation remains: for at once in verses 13 and 14 he will prove that Adam's sin is imputed to all, because all are sentenced to death. If you deny it, you do indeed remove the circle; but neither did Doctor Garissoles deny that, nor did he attempt anything of the kind in order to lead himself out of that circle: he therefore did the very thing of which he falsely accused us — he made of the divine Apostle, as he speaks, an inept circular arguer.

source_text: Sed tamen inde hoc argumentum elicit. Quibus irrogatur poena mortis propter peccatum, iis peccatum imputatur. Atqui infantibus irrogata est ante legem poena mortis propter peccatum Adae. Ergo iis peccatum Adae imputatum est. Resp. Peccatum Adae duobus modis accipi: 1. pro eo peccato, quod ab eo in posteros propagatum & secundum hominum numerum multiplicatum, caro & vetus Adam appellatur. 2. pro causa peccati illius propagati, nempe actuali Adae inobedientia. Si priore modo accipitur, concedo totum argumentum. Fateor enim peccatum illud, quia intra nos est, nobis omnibus, etiam infantibus, merito imputari. Si posteriore modo, distinguo praepositionem propter: nam vel causam proximam seu immediatam, vel remotam tantum seu mediatam significat. Si prius, nego minorem propositionem: irrogata est infantibus poena mortis proxime ob inhaerens vitium, remote ob Adami actuale peccatum. Si posterius, inde sequitur duntaxat peccati illius actualis imputatio mediata, quam ultro concedo. Hoc me docuit Calvinus, quia, inquit, ejus peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus ascribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur. Et Bullingerus, non noceret nobis Adae lapsus, nisi talis ex eo perversitas seu corruptio nobis innata fuisset, quae Dei judicium promeretur.
english: Yet from there he draws out this argument: "To those on whom the penalty of death is inflicted on account of sin, sin is imputed. But before the law the penalty of death on account of Adam's sin was inflicted on infants. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them." I answer: Adam's sin is taken in two ways: (1) for that sin which, propagated from him into posterity and multiplied according to the number of men, is called flesh and the old Adam; (2) for the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If it is taken in the former way, I grant the whole argument. For I confess that that sin, because it is within us, is rightly imputed to us all, even to infants. If in the latter way, I distinguish the preposition "on account of": for it signifies either the near or immediate cause, or only the remote or mediate. If the former, I deny the minor proposition: the penalty of death was inflicted on infants immediately on account of the inherent vice, remotely on account of Adam's actual sin. If the latter, there follows only a mediate imputation of that actual sin, which I freely grant. Calvin taught me this, because, he says, Adam's sin is the cause of our sin, and Paul ascribes our ruin to him (Romans 5). "I call our sin," he says, "that which is inborn in us, and with which we are born." And Bullinger: "Adam's fall would not hurt us unless such perversity or corruption had been inborn in us from it as would deserve God's judgment" (Decades).

source_text: Sic vindicata est versio Gallica, qua utuntur Ecclesiae nostrae. Quod autem subjungit D. G. Sic acriter disputatum fuisse, &c, sed ab eo tempore deferbuisse impetum, in posterioribus scriptis mutata esse velificationem &c, Fallitur vehementer. Eadem enim perpetuo Placei sententia fuit, & melius verti voces ἐφ᾽ ᾧ eo quod, quam in quo. Et tamen ne hanc quidem versionem obesse sententiae suae, ob eas rationes, quas thesibus suis aliquot annis, priusquam Manuscriptum illud prius fieret, editis, inseruerat. Non viderat illud manuscriptum, cum suum istud fecit quod D. G. posterius appellat, nec cur mutaret, ut loquitur vir Doctus, velificationem causa ulla erat. Nemo enim ei tum quicquam objecerat, quo recepta, quam sequitur, vocularum ἐφ᾽ ᾧ versio impugnaretur. De nostra confessione, quam praeter rationem triumphet hoc loco D. G. patet ex dictis pag. hujus lib. 73. Quae tamen si ulla fuisset, Placeo obesse non posset, quo inscio nec consentiente facta fuisset. Sed de illa versione jam fortasse plus satis.
english: Thus the French version used by our churches is vindicated. But as for what Doctor Garissoles subjoins — that it had been fiercely disputed, and so on, but that from that time the heat cooled, that in later writings the tack was changed, and so on (§ XIX, p. 239) — he is vehemently mistaken. For Placeus's judgment was the same throughout, and the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ are better rendered "because" than "in whom." And yet not even this version harms his position, for those reasons which he had inserted in his theses published some years before that earlier manuscript was made. He had not seen that manuscript when he made that piece of his which Doctor Garissoles calls later, nor was there any cause why he should change tack, as the learned man speaks. For no one had then objected anything to him by which the received version of the little words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, which he follows, could be attacked. As for our confession, over which Doctor Garissoles triumphs beyond reason in this place, it is plain from what was said at page 73 of this book. And yet if there had been any, it could not hurt Placeus, since it would have been made without his knowledge or consent. But of that version perhaps already more than enough.

source_text: Redeo ad argumentum supra pag. 70. ita propositum, ut ejus tres lineae a Typographo repetitae fuerint, nec a Correctore, adeo aliis distractus negotiis tunc festinabat, deletae. Id sic habet. Qui, cum nondum essent in rerum natura, dicuntur in alio peccasse, censentur proculdubio eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod evidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cum nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo peccasse. Ergo censentur eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi commisisse, quod ad imputationem peccati Adae manifeste pertinet. Primo nego id evidenter ad imputationem pertinere quam antecedentem seu immediatam voco. Cur enim non pertineat potius ad propagationem peccati inhaerentis, quod reatus & imputatio sequitur? Deinde nego majorem. An enim qui dicuntur in alio fuisse, vel mortui fuisse, censentur eo existente vel moriente & ipsi extitisse, & mortui fuisse? Morimur certe in Adamo, sed sua quisque morte; sicut resurgimus in Christo sua quisque resurrectione. Sic peccamus in Adamo, sed suo quisque peccato. Notatur tantum peccati & mortis primus autor & fons, unde ad nos omnes dimanarunt. Denique nego minorem. Non enim dixit Apostolus, omnes homines, cum nondum essent, in Adamo peccasse. Jam ostendi, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ non significare hoc loco in quo. Dixit quidem per unum hominem peccatum ita in mundum intrasse, ut omnes homines peccaverint, sed non dixit, peccasse in uno illo homine: Multo vero minus dixit tunc peccasse cum nondum essent in rerum natura. Hoc enim mihi videtur manifestam contradictionem implicare. Quis enim contradictionem implicari non videat, si quis dicat, prius esse accidens quam subjectum, prius homines fuisse peccatores quam homines, mortuos quam viventes, imo prius peccasse quam fuisse?
english: I return to the argument set out above at page 70 — so proposed that three of its lines were repeated by the typographer and not deleted by the corrector, so hurried was he then, distracted by other business. It runs thus: "Those who, when they were not yet in the nature of things, are said to have sinned in another are doubtless counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves also, which plainly pertains to imputation. But all men, when they were not yet, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves, which plainly pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin." First I deny that this plainly pertains to the imputation which I call antecedent or immediate. For why should it not rather pertain to the propagation of inherent sin, which guilt and imputation follow? Next I deny the major. For are those who are said to have been in another, or to have died, counted, while he existed or died, to have existed themselves and to have died? We certainly die in Adam, but each by his own death; just as we rise in Christ, each by his own resurrection. So we sin in Adam, but each by his own sin. Only the first author and fountain of sin and death is marked, from which they flowed out to us all. Finally I deny the minor. For the Apostle did not say that all men, when they were not yet, sinned in Adam. I have already shown that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ does not mean "in whom" in this place. He did say that through one man sin so entered into the world that all men sinned, but he did not say that they sinned in that one man: and much less did he say that they then sinned when they were not yet in the nature of things. For this seems to me to imply a plain contradiction. For who would not see a contradiction implied if someone should say that the accident was before the subject, that men were sinners before they were men, dead before living — indeed, that they sinned before they existed?

source_text:
CAPUT VIII.
Argumenta D. Gar. ex Rom. V. versibus 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. expenduntur.

Ex versu 14. hunc nectit Syllogismum. Ea est inter typum & τὸ ἀντίτυπον convenientia, ut quod in re per typum representata exhibetur, illud in typo praecessisse oportuerit. Atqui Adamus proponitur ut typus Christi in iis quae ad rationem iustificationis pertinent; ut nempe simili modo condemnationem habeamus in Adamo, quo iustificationem habemus in Christo. Itaque cum ea sit ratio iustificationis nostrae per Christum, ut eius iustitia nobis per imputationem communicata iustificemur, sive pro iustis habeamur apud Deum; Eam etiam oportet esse condemnationis per Adamum nostrae rationem, ut illius peccato nobis per imputationem communicato condemnemur, & pro peccatoribus ac reis habeamur apud Deum. Principio quacunque sit hujus argumenti vis, eo nonnisi consequens seu mediata imputatio concludi potest. Nam ut imputatio iustitiae sequitur fidem nostram, sic imputatio peccati sequitur corruptionem nostram. Hoc si sufficit, pax esto.
english: CAPUT VIII. The arguments of D. Garissoles from Romans 5, verses 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 are examined.

From verse 14 he joins this syllogism: There is this agreement between the type and the antitype (τὸ ἀντίτυπον), that what is exhibited in the thing represented by the type must have gone before in the type. But Adam is proposed as the type of Christ in those things that belong to the account of justification — namely that we should have condemnation in Adam in a like way to that in which we have justification in Christ (Romans 5:14). Therefore, since the account of our justification through Christ is that, his righteousness being communicated to us by imputation, we are justified, or are counted just before God, that must also be the account of our condemnation through Adam: that, his sin being communicated to us by imputation, we are condemned, and are counted sinners and guilty before God. First, whatever force this argument has, only consequent or mediate imputation can be concluded from it. For as the imputation of righteousness follows our faith, so the imputation of sin follows our corruption. If this is enough, let there be peace.

source_text: Deinde nullo negotio dissolvi potest hoc argumentum. Ad majorem enim quod attinet, propositio, Quod in re per typum representata exhibetur, illud in typo praecessisse oportuit. Eget hac limitatione, si nempe ad id representandum typus fuit comparatus. Nam alioqui saepenumero multa in re representata exhibita fuerunt, quae non potuerunt uno typo representari; quapropter multi ad eandem rem adumbrandam adhibiti sunt. Deinde etiam adhibita illa limitatione propositio vera non est, nisi quantum pati potest ejus rei, quae typus est, natura, servata inter Typum & τὸ ἀντίτυπον, umbram & corpus differentia. Itaque melior est a typo ad rem adumbratam, quam ab hac ad illam argumentatio.
english: Next, this argument can be dissolved without any trouble. For as to the major: the proposition "What is exhibited in the thing represented by a type must have preceded in the type" needs this limitation — if, that is, the type was set up to represent that thing. For otherwise often many things have been exhibited in the represented matter which could not be represented by one type; and for that reason several have been employed to sketch the same thing. Then even when that limitation is applied, the proposition is not true except so far as the nature of the thing which is the type can bear, the difference between Type and antitype (τὸ ἀντίτυπον), shadow and body, being kept. Therefore argumentation from the type to the thing shadowed is better than from this latter back to the former.

source_text: Ad minorem autem quod spectat, jam aliquoties negavimus urgeri debere similitudinem in modo, quo ab Adamo condemnationem, & a Christo iustificationem habemus. Idque cum autoritate magnorum virorum, tum aliquot exemplis comprobavimus. Audi, si placet, Calvinum, Porro duas hic differentias inter Christum & Adamum notare operae pretium est: quas non ideo praeteriit Apostolus, quia negligendas censeret, sed quia praesentis argumenti nihil referebat eas enumerare. Prior est quod peccato Adae non per solam imputationem damnamur, ac si alieni peccati exigeretur a nobis poena: sed ideo poenam eius sustinemus, quia & culpae sumus rei, quatenus scilicet natura nostra in ipso vitiata, iniquitatis reatu astringitur apud Deum. At per Christi iustitiam alio modo in salutem restituimur: neque enim ideo nobis accepta fertur, quia intra nos sit: sed quod Christum ipsum cum bonis suis omnibus, Patris largitate nobis donatum possidemus. Itaque donum iustitiae, non qualitatem qua nos Deus imbuat, ut perperam quidam interpretantur, sed gratuitam iustitiae imputationem significat.
english: But as to the minor: we have already denied several times that the likeness must be pressed in the mode by which we have condemnation from Adam and justification from Christ. And we have confirmed this both by the authority of great men and by several examples. Hear Calvin, if you please: "Further, it is worth noting here two differences between Christ and Adam: which the Apostle did not omit because he judged them negligible, but because it did not serve the present argument to enumerate them. The first is that we are not damned by Adam's sin through imputation alone, as if the penalty of another's sin were being exacted from us: but we therefore bear his penalty because we are also guilty of the fault, inasmuch as our nature, corrupted in him, is bound before God under the guilt of iniquity. But by Christ's righteousness we are restored to salvation in another way: for it is not therefore credited to us because it is within us, but because we possess Christ himself with all his goods, given to us by the Father's bounty. And so the gift of righteousness signifies not a quality with which God imbues us, as some wrongly interpret, but the free imputation of righteousness."

source_text: Placet-ne etiam audire Rodolphum Gualterum? Sensus ergo est, in hoc quidem comparari inter se posse Adamum & Christum, quod uterque quod suum erat in suos propagarit. In caeteris vero Multiplex esse discrimen, neque eandem esse rationem offensae aut peccati per Adamum invecti, & beneficii nobis in Christo exhibiti &c. & paulo post. Videtur autem duplex discrimen his verbis annotari, ut primo quidem Natura corrupta & gratia Dei opponantur, eo quod Adam quidem propter naturae corruptionem, quam ex suo lapsu contraxit, peccatum in omnes posteros propagarit, adeo ut peccatores ex ipso matris utero nascamur: Christus vero nobis ex gratia datus sit, ut eius iustitia sive obedientia in multos, id est, in omnes redundaret. Quod ergo peccatores & propter peccatum morti obnoxii sumus, hoc ex natura ceu proprium habemus: quod vero iusti & vitae consortes facti sumus, id gratuitum Dei beneficium est, qui Filii sui iustitiam nobis imputat propter fidem, qua hunc apprehendimus. His duobus tertium adiungam Petrum Martyrem Com. in Rom. 5. Vs. 14. ad verba qui est typus futuri. Similitudo haec accipienda est in genere quod sicut omnes ab Adamo, ita omnes a Christo iuxta ordinem suum pendeant: quodque quemadmodum alter meritus est suis omnibus, ita etiam alter. Sed particulariter & quoad species magnum est discrimen. Nam Adamus peccatum, mortem, & damnationem invexit: Christus vero iustitiam, vitam & gratiam. Est etiam discrimen in propagatione. Adamus enim mala sua per carnis generationem in homines transfudit. Christus autem per fidem. Ideo Paulus cum dixisset, Adamum typum fuisse futuri, quasi per correctionem subiicit. At non ut peccatum, ita & donum. Quamobrem inter Adamum & Christum potius analogia quaedam & proportio, quam vera similitudo constituenda est. Vides nos Magnorum virorum doctrinam adversus D. Garissolii impetum defendere. Noli nos igitur quaeso, candide lector, novitatis damnare.
english: Does it please you also to hear Rudolph Gualther? "The sense, then, is that Adam and Christ can indeed be compared with each other in this, that each propagated into his own what was his. But in the rest there is a manifold difference, and the account of the offense or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as that of the benefit exhibited to us in Christ," and so on. And a little later: "But a double difference seems to be noted in these words, so that first corrupt Nature and the grace of God are opposed, because Adam indeed, on account of the corruption of nature which he contracted from his fall, propagated sin into all posterity, so that we are born sinners from the very womb of our mother: but Christ was given to us by grace, so that his righteousness or obedience should overflow into the many, that is, into all. Therefore that we are sinners and liable to death because of sin, we have from nature as our own: but that we have been made just and sharers of life is the free benefit of God, who imputes to us the righteousness of his Son because of the faith by which we apprehend him." To these two I will add a third, Peter Martyr, Commentary on Romans 5:14, at the words "who is the type of the one to come" (Romans 5:14): "This likeness is to be taken in the genus, that as all depend on Adam, so all depend on Christ according to their order: and that as the one has merited for all who are his, so also the other. But particularly and as to the species there is a great difference. For Adam brought in sin, death, and damnation: but Christ righteousness, life, and grace. There is also a difference in the propagation. For Adam poured his evils into men by the generation of the flesh. But Christ by faith. Therefore when Paul had said that Adam was the type of the one to come, he subjoins as if by correction: But not as the sin, so also the gift (Romans 5:15). So between Adam and Christ an analogy and proportion of a certain kind, rather than a true likeness, is to be established." You see us defending the teaching of great men against the assault of D. Garissoles. Do not therefore, I ask, candid reader, condemn us for novelty.

source_text: II. Ex Vs. 15. At non ut lapsus, ita etiam donum &c. sic colligit; Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxii, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii. Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Facilis est responsio. Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxii proxime seu immediate, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati proxime seu immediate. Qui eo peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii tantum remote seu mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione, illi ferunt poenas illius peccati tantum remote seu mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii proxime seu immediate, Nego: mediante corruptione, Concedo. Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur, immediate, nego: mediante corruptione nobis inhaerente, Concedo. Nonne omnia D. Gar. argumenta hac una fidelia dealbari possunt?
english: II. From verse 15, "But not as the fall, so also the gift," and so on (Romans 5:15), he gathers thus: Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them. But all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin. Therefore all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them. The reply is easy. Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately bear the penalty of that sin proximately or immediately. Those who by that sin have been made liable to death only remotely or mediately — that is, by intervening corruption — bear the penalties of that sin only remotely or mediately, that is, by intervening corruption. But that all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately — I deny; by intervening corruption — I grant. Therefore that all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them, immediately — I deny; by the corruption inhering in us — I grant. Cannot all the arguments of D. Garissoles be whitewashed with this one brush?

source_text: Deinde, inquit, opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. At per χάρισμα intelligitur iustitia illa Christi, quae gratiosa imputatione fit nostra, & quae sanctificationem, sive iustitiam inhaerentem ex se necessario fundit. Ergo & παράπτωμα intelligitur peccatum illud Adami, quod imputatione nostrum fit, & quod corruptio nostra naturalis necessario & infallibiliter sequitur. Omnino opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. Quid inde sequitur? Nonne jam aliquoties argumento ducto ab hac oppositione occurrimus? Caeterum aut anomalus est hic syllogismus, nec vim ullam concludendi habet, aut omissa est propositio, quae si universaliter, ut debet, concipiatur, erit falsa procul dubio. Admonet autem nos oppositio inter παράπτωμα Adami & χάρισμα Christi, longe aliter hoc nostrum esse quam illud. Non enim, ut hoc nostrum est dono Christi, sic illud est nostrum dono Adami. Alterum ergo alteri opponit Apostolus in modo quo fit nostrum. Quomodo igitur ex hac oppositione concludere potest D. G. utrumque eodem modo nostrum fieri? Dicet-ne imputationem, qua aliquid nostrum fit, alioqui non nostrum, esse donationem quandam. Est igitur Adami peccatum donum quoddam, non Adami, hic enim non imputat; sed, horresco pronuncians, ipsius Dei.
english: Next, he says, the Apostle sets opposite Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα (Romans 5:15). But by χάρισμα is understood that righteousness of Christ which becomes ours by gracious imputation, and which necessarily pours forth from itself sanctification, or inhering righteousness. Therefore by παράπτωμα also is understood that sin of Adam which becomes ours by imputation, and which our natural corruption necessarily and infallibly follows. Entirely so: the Apostle does set opposite Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα. What follows from that? Have we not already met several times an argument drawn from this opposition? For the rest, either this syllogism is irregular and has no force of concluding, or a proposition has been omitted which, if it is conceived universally as it ought to be, will without doubt be false. But the opposition between Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα warns us that this which is ours is far otherwise than that. For it is not that, as this is ours by the gift of Christ, so that is ours by the gift of Adam. Therefore the Apostle sets the one opposite the other in the mode by which it becomes ours. How then can D. Garissoles conclude from this opposition that both become ours in the same mode? Will he say that imputation, by which something becomes ours which otherwise is not ours, is a kind of donation? Then Adam's sin is a kind of gift — not Adam's, for he does not impute; but, I shudder to pronounce it, God's own.

source_text: Hic D. G. insignem Calvini locum jam a nobis laudatum pag. 20. contra se citat. Quod unius delicto periisse nos tradit, sic accipe, quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa sit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa, quasi extra culpam ipsi simus; Sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Non potuit apertius significare, peccatum Adami causam esse exitii nostri non proximam sed remotam, non immediatam, sed mediatam. Causa enim causae est causa etiam effectus, sed remota duntaxat.
english: Here D. Garissoles turns against himself a distinguished place of Calvin that we already praised at page 20. "What he hands down — that we perished by the offense of one — take thus: because from him corruption was poured across into us. For we do not so perish by his fault as if we ourselves were outside fault; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him" (Romans 5:15). He could not have marked more openly that Adam's sin is the cause of our ruin not proximate but remote, not immediate but mediate. For the cause of a cause is also a cause of the effect, yet only remote.

source_text: Conatur tamen tam claro loco tenebras offundere D. G. Quibus verbis, inquit, non negatur nos Adami ipsius actuali peccato perire, nec hoc etiam negat, aut negavit unquam Placeus: Sed significatur, non esse illud Adami peccatum a nostra corruptione separandum, quippe cum ex utroque confurgat idem reatus. An id verbis illis significetur, eaque ratio afferatur, iudicium esto penes Lectorem. Illud mihi satis est,
english: Yet D. Garissoles tries to cast darkness over a place so clear. "By which words," he says, "it is not denied that we perish by Adam's own actual sin" — and Placeus neither denies this nor has ever denied it — "but it is signified that that sin of Adam is not to be parted from our corruption, seeing that from both the same guilt rises together." Whether those words signify that, and whether that reason is brought, let judgment rest with the Reader. This is enough for me:

source_text: ideo exitium nostrum Adami peccato adscribi, quia est causa peccati nostri, non dicit, quia nobis imputatur, aut quia imputatione nostrum est: sed illud distinguit a peccato nostro tanquam causam ab effectu. Est igitur a peccato Adami peccatum nostrum, & ab hoc exitium nostrum. Ita ex utroque confurgit idem reatus, ex peccato nostro proxime, ex peccato Adami remote.
english: that our ruin is ascribed to Adam's sin because it is the cause of our sin. He does not say, because it is imputed to us, or because it is ours by imputation; but he distinguishes that from our sin as cause from effect. Therefore our sin is from Adam's sin, and from this our ruin. So from both the same guilt rises — from our sin proximately, from Adam's sin remotely.

source_text: Exponit mentem suam alibi Calvinus, Peccatum originale, inquit, est naturae nostrae pravitas ac corruptio, quae primum reos facit nos irae Dei, tum etiam opera in nobis profert quae Scriptura vocat opera carnis. Sequitur ergo reatus corruptionem ut effectus causam, & quidem causam, ut loquuntur, adaequatam: subiungit enim continuo. Haec itaque duo distincte observanda: nempe quod sic omnibus naturae nostrae partibus vitiati perversique, iam ob talem duntaxat corruptionem damnati merito convictique coram Deo tenemur. Quae eadem verba, adeo tanto viro placebant, bis extant in ejus institutione, semel lib. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. & iterum lib. 4. cap. 15. §. 10.
english: Elsewhere Calvin unfolds his mind. "Original sin," he says, "is the depravity and corruption of our nature, which first makes us guilty of the wrath of God, then also brings forth in us works which Scripture calls works of the flesh" (Galatians 5:19). Therefore guilt follows corruption as effect follows cause — and indeed, as they say, an adequate cause: for he subjoins at once. "These two things, then, are to be observed distinctly: namely that, being thus spoiled and perverted in all the parts of our nature, we are already held before God justly damned and convicted on account of that corruption alone." Which same words so pleased so great a man that they stand twice in his Institutes — once in book 2, chapter 1, section 8, and again in book 4, chapter 15, section 10.

source_text: Addit quoque in priore loco uberioris explicationis gratia haec verba. Neque ista est alieni delicti obligatio: quod enim dicitur, nos per Adae peccatum obnoxios esse factos Dei judicio: non ita est accipiendum, ac si insones ipsi & immerentes culpam delicti ejus sustineremus: sed quia per eius transgressionem maledictione induti sumus omnes, dicitur ille nos obstrinxisse. Ab illo tamen non sola in nos poena grassata est, sed instillata ab ipso lues in nobis residet cui iure poena debetur. Quare Augustinus utcunque alienum peccatum saepe vocet (quo clarius ostendat propagine in nos derivari) simul tamen & proprium unicuique asserit. Et Apostolus ipse disertissime testatur, ideo mortem in omnes pervagatam, quod omnes peccarint, id est, involuti sint originali peccato, & eius maculis inquinati. Atque adeo infantes quoque ipsi, dum suam secum damnationem a matris utero afferunt, non alieno, sed suo ipsorum vitio sunt obstricti. Reatus igitur & damnatio & mors sequuntur corruptionem haereditariam ut effectus causam, & ob eam duntaxat non autem ob peccatum actuale Adami (nisi remote & mediate) morti sumus addicti.
english: He also adds in the earlier place, for fuller explanation, these words. "Nor is this an obligation of another's offense: for what is said — that by Adam's sin we have been made liable to God's judgment — is not to be taken as if we ourselves, innocent and undeserving, were bearing the blame of his offense; but because through his transgression we have all been clothed with the curse, he is said to have bound us. Yet from him not penalty alone has rushed upon us, but a plague poured in from him resides in us, to which penalty is due by right. So Augustine, however often he may call it another's sin (so that he may show more clearly that it is derived into us by propagation), yet at the same time asserts it also as each one's own. And the Apostle himself most expressly testifies that death has wandered through unto all for this reason, that all have sinned — that is, that they have been wrapped in original sin and stained with its spots" (Romans 5:12). And so even infants themselves, while they bring with them their damnation from the mother's womb, are bound not by another's vice but by their own. Therefore guilt and condemnation and death follow hereditary corruption as effect follows cause, and on account of that alone — not, however, on account of Adam's actual sin (except remotely and mediately) — we are sentenced to death.

source_text: III. Ex verf. 16. sic ratiocinatur. Hic κρίμα, judicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur δώρημα Christi. Ergo ut δώρημα non significat qualitatem aliquam nobis inherentem, sed quod in Christo est, & in Christo nobis gratis imputatur; Ita κρίμα aliquid significare debet, quod sit extra nos, nempe culpam ab Adamo patratam, unde reatum & condemnationem trahimus. Collige. Cujus culpa est in omnium condemnationem, eam omnibus imputari oportet. Atqui culpa Adami est in omnium condemnationem. Ergo eam omnibus imputari oportet.
english: III. From verse 16 he reasons thus. Here κρίμα, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set opposite Christ's δώρημα (Romans 5:16). Therefore, as δώρημα does not signify some quality inhering in us, but what is in Christ, and is freely imputed to us in Christ, so κρίμα must signify something outside us — namely the fault committed by Adam, from which we draw guilt and condemnation. Collect: Whose fault is unto the condemnation of all, that fault must be imputed to all. But Adam's fault is unto the condemnation of all. Therefore it must be imputed to all.

source_text: Nihil roboris in hoc argumento video, quod non extet in superioribus jam abundè refutatis. Quae enim & quam imbecilla est haec collectio; Hic κρίμα judicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur δώρημα Christi. Ergo ut hoc non significat qualitatem nobis inhaerentem, sic nec illud?
english: I see no strength in this argument that is not already present in the earlier ones, now amply refuted. For how weak this collection is: Here κρίμα, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set opposite Christ's δώρημα. Therefore, as the one does not signify a quality inhering in us, neither does the other?

source_text: Quid enim prohibet, vitium inhaerens quatenus nos facit reos & poena dignos ei justitiae opponi, quae nos ab eo reatu & poena liberat, uti vidimus censuisse maximos viros? Id non modo nihil prohibet, sed ipsa illa oppositio exigit. Est enim κρίμα ex justitia, δώρημα ex gratia. Justitia nonnisi suum cuique tribuit; gratia donat id quod alioqui nostrum non erat, sed alienum.
english: For what forbids an inhering vice, insofar as it makes us guilty and worthy of penalty, from being set opposite that justice which frees us from that guilt and penalty — as we have seen the greatest men judged? Not only does nothing forbid it; that very opposition requires it. For κρίμα is from justice, δώρημα from grace. Justice assigns to each only what is his own; grace gives what was otherwise not ours, but another's.

source_text: Hoc accepi a Chamiero, Si nihil, inquit, habent infantes peccati proprii, cur propria morte pereunt? Nam propter alienam culpam, quae tantum aliena sit, non fert justitia divina. Habuerint sane aliquando homines eum morem, ut patris servitus, filiis esset hereditaria: at ejusmodi nihil erat in populo Dei, ex divinis legibus: quanto minus in Deo: qui irascitur in eos, quibus erat in ore proverbium, Patres nostri uvas acerbas comederunt: Filiis autem dentes stupent;
english: I took this from Chamier. "If infants," he says, "have nothing of their own sin, why do they perish by their own death? For divine justice does not bear an alien fault that is only alien. Men may once have had the custom that a father's slavery was hereditary for the sons; but nothing of that kind stood in the people of God under the divine laws — how much less in God, who is angry at those who had in their mouth the proverb, Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (Ezekiel 18:2).

source_text: Quod si excipiat quis, servari fideles propter justitiam non suam, sed Christi: itaque posse etiam damnari, propter alienam injustitiam, is vero non videt comparari valde diversa. Nam damnatio est a justitia, salus autem a gratia. Nam si esset etiam ipsa a justitia, non posset nos aliena justitia servare: quare ne aliena quidem culpa damnare. Nihil, opinor, desiderari potuit disertius.
english: But if someone objects that the faithful are saved on account of a righteousness not their own but Christ's, and that therefore they can also be damned on account of an alien injustice, he truly does not see that very different things are being compared. For damnation is from justice, but salvation is from grace. For if salvation itself were also from justice, an alien righteousness could not save us; so neither can an alien guilt damn. Nothing, I think, could have been wanted more expressly.

source_text: IV. Veniamus igitur ad verf. 17. Ex eo simile, inquit D. G. argumentum emergit. Cuius delicto & lapsu mors semper regnavit & regnatura est in finem seculi, eius delicti poena pervadit in omnes. Mors enim certe ab Apostolo ponitur, tanquam causae illius effectum. At uno Adami delicto mors hactenus in omnes regnavit, & porro regnatura est usque ad finem seculi. Igitur delicti & lapsus illius Adae poena in omnes pervagatur.
english: IV. Let us come, then, to verse 17. From it, says D. Garissoles, a similar argument arises. The one by whose offense and fall death has always reigned and will reign to the end of the age — that one's offense-penalty pervades all. For death is certainly set by the Apostle as the effect of that cause (Romans 5:17). But by one offense of Adam death has so far reigned over all, and will go on reigning to the end of the age. Therefore the penalty of that offense and fall of Adam pervades all.

source_text: Concedo totum arg. Quis enim nostrum unquam negavit, lapsus Adae poenam in omnes esse pervagatam? Tantum contendimus, inter eam & lapsum Adae intervenisse vitium originale cui proxime poena debetur.
english: I grant the whole argument. Which of us ever denied that the penalty of Adam's fall has pervaded all? We contend only this: between that penalty and Adam's fall, original vice has intervened, and to that vice the penalty is owed proximately.

source_text: Est igitur lapsus Adae prima causa regni mortis, sed proxima est ab illo productum peccatum omnibus inhaerens, quod quia regnat, etiam mors regnat. Certe peccatum quod in hominibus non modo est, sed vivit; non modo vivit sed regnat; cui serviunt, cui obediunt, cujus lex est in membris. Id non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed hujus effectum, corruptio inhaerens.
english: So Adam's fall is the first cause of death's reign, but the proximate cause is the sin produced from it and inhering in all; and because that sin reigns, death also reigns. Certainly the sin in human beings not only is, but lives; not only lives but reigns — the sin they serve, the sin they obey, whose law is in their members. That is not Adam's actual sin, but its effect: inhering corruption.

source_text: V. Ex verf. 18. simili ratione ac supra colligit.
