Ego vero (pace tua & aliorum, qui sic tecum sentiunt,) non possum verba illa morte morieris ad mortem spiritualem seu privationem justitiae & sanctitatis transferre. Audi, si placet, rationes meas, & expende: nam, nisi me fallit animus, non sunt de nihilo. Prima ratio. Comminatio opponitur tacite promissioni, poena praemio, mors denunciata vitae promissae. Atqui vita tacite promissa Adamo non erat justitia seu sanctitas, nisi velis promissionis conditionem cum re promissa confundere. Ergo mors denunciata non erat privatio justitiae.
english: Against this threefold life you set a threefold privation or death, denounced by God to Adam as penalty in the words "you shall die the death," and you claim that man was dead just as God had threatened. For my part (with leave of you and of those who think with you) I cannot shift those words onto spiritual death—the loss of justice and sanctity. Hear my reasons, if you will, and weigh them; unless I am mistaken, they are not empty.

First reason. A threat answers a tacit promise, penalty answers reward, the death denounced answers the life promised. But the life tacitly promised to Adam was not justice or sanctity—unless you confuse the condition of the promise with the thing promised. Therefore the death denounced was not the privation of justice.

source_text: GAR. Resp. Minorem non esse simpliciter veram, si audiatur Camero praelect. de verbo Dei cap. 7. Summum hominis bonum est animi & corporis, adeoque totius hominis status perfectus atque omnibus numeris absolutus, nihil ut ultra requiri vel debeat, vel possit amplius. Hic vero status & conditio est imago Dei. Ceterum imago Dei in duobus sita est, in sanctitate, & qua sanctitatem sequitur, beata immortalitate. Si vita promissa Adae erat status ipsius perfectus, & ea vita consistit in sanctitate. Ergo vita promissa consistebat in sanctitate. Nec aliter Clar. Amyraldus, De trib. foeder. Thes. II. Promissio foederis illius primi consistere debuit in vita perpetua, & affluente omni bonorum genere, qua tum in animum, tum in corpus hominis competere potuissent. Justitia autem & sanctitas nonne inter animi bona censeri debent?
english: GAR. Reply. The minor is not simply true, if one hears Cameron, Lectures on the Word of God, chapter 7: "Man's highest good is a perfect state of soul and body—of the whole man—complete in every respect, so that nothing further can or ought to be asked. This state and condition is the image of God. The image of God sits in two things: sanctity, and the blessed immortality that follows sanctity." If the life promised to Adam was his perfect state, and that life consists in sanctity, then the promised life consisted in sanctity.

Nor does the most illustrious Amyraut speak otherwise, On the Three Covenants, Thesis II: "The promise of that first covenant had to consist in perpetual life, abounding in every kind of good that could belong to man's mind and body." But ought not justice and sanctity to be counted among the goods of the mind?

source_text: PLAC. Quis non videt a praestantissimo Camerone describi eo loco, non vitam quatenus promissa Adamo sub perfectae obedientiae conditione fuerat, sed absolute summum hominis bonum, quale Dei verbo seu Euangelio promittitur? Differt autem admodum id quod foedere gratiae promittitur, ab eo quod foedere naturae promittebatur Adamo. Quis etiam non videt, Clariss. Collegam D. Amyraldum bona intelligere, ut ita loquar, physica, non autem ea quae mere moralia erant, quorumque continuatio exigebatur ab Adamo?
english: PLAC. Who does not see that the most excellent Cameron is describing there not the life promised to Adam under the condition of perfect obedience, but absolutely man's highest good as the Word of God—or the Gospel—promises it? What the covenant of grace promises differs sharply from what the covenant of nature was promising Adam.
Who also does not see that our most illustrious colleague Amyraut means, so to speak, physical goods—not the merely moral ones whose continuance God was requiring of Adam?

source_text: Itaque inseruerat haec verba, in statu integrae naturae constituti, & subiunxerat ista eaque in paradiso Terrestri fruenda, quae cur sint a Viro Docto omissa, aliis judicandum relinquo. Innuunt certe supponi integritatis moralis Naturae conservationem, promitti reliquorum omnium bonorum in paradiso Terrestri fruendorum continuationem. Nam, ut Minorem negatam probem, si comminabatur Deus Adamo tanquam poenam, amissionem seu privationem justitiae originalis, certe pollicebatur tanquam praemium, non-amissionem seu conservationem justitiae originalis, quomodo igitur fieri potuit ut eam Adamus amitteret? Pollicebatur, inquies, sub conditione. Quanam? si perseveraret in integritate & justitia? Si permaneret in obedientia erga Deum? Si non peccaret? Quocunque nomine eam voces, idem erit cum re promissa, & conditio promissionis cum re promissa confundetur.
english: So Amyraut had inserted the words "constituted in the state of integral nature," and had added "and those things to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise"—why the learned man omitted them I leave others to judge. They clearly presuppose conservation of nature's moral integrity and promise continuance of the remaining goods to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise.

To prove the denied minor: if God threatened Adam, as penalty, with loss or privation of original justice, then as reward He was promising non-loss—conservation—of that justice. How then could Adam lose it? "He promised under a condition," you say. Which? If he persevered in integrity and justice? Remained obedient to God? Did not sin? Call it what you will: it is the same as the thing promised, and the condition of the promise is confused with the thing promised.

source_text: GAR. Hoc iterum inficiamur. Quia justitia & sanctitas Adami duplex constitui potest. Altera naturalis, altera supernaturalis: altera viae, altera patriae; altera hominis creati, altera hominis glorificati. Justitia naturalis & hominis creati quae justitia viae dici potest, erat conditio promissionis; sed supernaturalis, & hominis glorificati, quam dicimus justitiam patriae, erat res promissa.
english: GAR. We deny this again. Adam's justice and sanctity admit a twofold account: natural versus supernatural; of the way versus of the homeland; of created man versus of glorified man.
Natural justice—created man's justice of the way—was only the condition of the promise. Supernatural justice—glorified man's justice of the homeland—was the thing promised.

source_text: PLAC. Hac responsione sibi Vir Doctus aperte contradicit, & cum videatur respondere, non respondet tamen, sed dat manus. Agebatur enim de justitia originali, ut patet ex meo argumento. Utra igitur duarum illarum, quas distinxit, justitiarum est justitia originalis? Num illa supernaturalis, patriae, hominis glorificati? Non certe. Non enim illa Adamus priusquam peccaret praeditus erat: non illam erat propagaturus in posteros. Est igitur justitia naturalis, viae, hominis creati, justitia originalis de qua agebatur in argumento? Atqui Vir doctus confitetur hanc Justitiam fuisse conditionem promissionis. Confitetur ergo non fuisse promissam: id quod probare institueram, & ipse negaverat. Quod si non fuit promissa, eius privatio non fuit mors comminatione denunciata. Id quod mihi probandum incumbebat.
english: PLAC. This answer openly contradicts the learned man himself. He seems to reply, yet does not—he yields. We were arguing about original justice, as my case shows. Of the two justices he split apart, which is original? The supernatural homeland justice of glorified man? No. Adam lacked that before the fall and was never going to hand it down.

So original justice in the argument is natural justice—of the way, of created man. But Garissoles admits that justice was the condition of the promise. He therefore admits it was not promised—the very point I meant to prove, which he had denied. If it was not promised, losing it was not the death the threat denounced. That is what I had to establish.

source_text: Ceterum libenter quaesiverim, unde habuerit Vir Doctus foedere naturae, cuius conditio fuit justitia naturalis, promissam fuisse justitiam supernaturalem? Id ne alicubi dicit Scriptura? An potest ratiocinando ex Naturae contemplatione colligi? Quaero etiam unde habuerit, Adami, qui e terra fuit, terrenus, & cuius paradisus fuit in terra, patriam non fuisse terram? Tollere certe videtur discrimen inter foedus naturae & foedus gratiae, primum hominem & secundum, & aliquid docere, immo Dei voluntatem quandam & promissionem confingere praeter Scripturam. Id quod omni Christiano, praecipue inter Reformatos Theologiae professori summa cura vitandum est.
english: Beyond that I would gladly know Garissoles' source for saying the covenant of nature—conditioned on natural justice—promised supernatural justice. Where does Scripture say so? Can bare contemplation of nature prove it by reasoning?

And where did he get the claim that Adam—earthly, from the earth, with an earthly paradise—did not have earth for his homeland? That erases the line between nature's covenant and grace's, between the first man and the second, and invents a divine will and promise beyond Scripture. No Christian—least of all a Reformed professor of theology—may risk that.

source_text: Secunda, Hoc potest illustrari & confirmari promissione & comminatione foederis legalis. Pollicebatur vitam, hoc fac & vives. Quam? spiritualem illam positam in justitia & sanctitate? nihil minus: eius nec initium, nec progressum, nec continuationem lex promittebat, sed exigebat. Promissiones foederis legalis erant conditionales. Conditio erat perfecta justitia perpetuo conservata. Sub hac conditione promittebatur vita. Quare vita promissa non potuit sita esse in praesentia justitiae. Iam autem mors, quam lex comminabatur, opposita erat formaliter non conditioni, sed vitae promissae: non consistebat igitur in absentia seu privatione justitiae.
english: Second proof. The legal covenant's own promise and threat make the same point. Life was pledged under the formula "do this and you will live." Was that the spiritual life grounded in righteousness and holiness? Far from it. The law never promised the start, growth, or continuance of that life; it demanded them. Legal-covenant promises were conditional, and the condition was perfect righteousness kept without break. Life was promised only under that condition—so the thing promised cannot have been identical with righteousness itself already present. And the death the law threatened stood formally over against the promised life, not against the condition. Hence that death was not the absence or stripping-away of righteousness.

source_text: PLAC. Hanc secundam rationem D. Garissolius alto Silentio praeteriit.
english: Placeus. Garissoles met this second argument with total silence.

source_text: Tertia, violatio conditionis sive praecepti non est poena transgressori denunciata. Sed privatio justitiae est violatio conditionis seu praecepti. Ergo non est poena transgressori denunciata. Major probatione non eget: Minorem sic demonstro. Quod lex prohibet, id legis violatio est. At lex prohibet absentiam justitiae in homine (tam certe quam jubet homini justitiam inesse.) Ergo absentia justitiae (quae tibi mors est spiritualis) violatio est legis.
english: Third proof: breaking the condition or precept is not itself the penalty announced against the breaker. But loss of righteousness is breaking the condition or precept. Therefore that loss is not the announced penalty. The major is obvious; I prove the minor as follows. Whatever the law forbids is a breach of the law. The law forbids righteousness being absent from a man as firmly as it commands righteousness to be in him. Therefore that absence—which you call spiritual death—is a breach of the law.

source_text: GAR. Respond. De majore litem hic non moveo: disputabitur inferius, an violatio praecepti divini, quae peccatum est, possit esse poena peccati. Ad minorem dico, distinguendam esse privationem justitiae, ut aliam activam nominemus, aliam passivam. Activa est, qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, qua Deus illum impertiverat: passiva qua Deus hominem justitia privat, & donis quibus ipsum cumularat. Si ergo agnoscimus privationem activam justitiae idem esse cum violatione legis; de privatione tamen passiva id merito negabitur.
english: Garissoles replies. I will not contest the major here; later we can ask whether breaking a divine precept (which is sin) can also be sin's penalty. On the minor I distinguish two privations of righteousness: active and passive. Active is the man's own bad acting by which he strips himself of the righteousness God had given him. Passive is God's stripping the man of that righteousness and of the gifts heaped on him. Grant that the active privation is the same as law-breaking; the passive still is not.

source_text: PLAC. Quod de majore litem hic non movet, prudenter facit: nam praeter tres illas rationes, quae sequuntur in Manuscripto, ad quas nihil respondit, violatio conditionis seu praecepti prima nec antecedentis peccati poena esse potest, cum sit peccatum primum, nec sui ipsius, cum non possit posterior esse seipsa: & ridicule apponeretur praecepto comminatio, quae minaretur fore ut violetur praeceptum, si violetur. Minorem argumento confirmaveram, quod illi visum est tutius silentio tegere, quam attingere. Potest etiam sic probari. Peccatum est violatio legis. Privatio justitiae in homine, est peccatum. Ergo privatio justitiae est violatio legis. Quid clarius? At ille distinguit privationem justitiae in activam & passivam: illam qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, hanc qua Deus hominem justitia privat: illam fatetur esse violationem legis, hanc negat. Ex quo sequitur, hanc, non illam, legem esse suo violatori comminatam. Consideremus igitur paulo attentius illam distinctionem. Recte sane privatio justitiae activa dicitur respectu privantis se justitia hominis: activa enim dicitur respectu agentis. Sed passiva, cur non similiter dicitur respectu privati seu patientis hominis? Nam ut privans respondet privato, agens patienti, actio passioni, ita videtur privatio active sumpta esse privantis, passive vero privati? Cur ergo passiva tribuitur Deo, qui privat hominem justitia, non privatur ullo modo? Hoc primum.
english: Placeus. He is wise not to fight the major here. Besides three further Manuscript reasons he never answered, the first breach of the condition cannot be the penalty of some earlier sin—because it is the first sin—nor the penalty of itself, since nothing is later than itself. It would be absurd to attach to a precept a threat that the precept will be broken if it is broken. I had already confirmed the minor by an argument he preferred to bury in silence rather than face. Another proof: sin is law-breaking; privation of righteousness in a man is sin; therefore that privation is law-breaking. Clearer still? Yet he splits privation into active and passive—the man's self-stripping versus God's stripping—and admits only the first as law-breaking. So on his view the threatened law-penalty is the second, not the first. Look harder at that split. "Active" rightly names privation from the agent's side—the man who strips himself. Why then is "passive" not named from the patient's side—the man stripped? Privating answers to privated, agent to patient, action to passion; so active privation belongs to the one who strips, passive to the one stripped. How then is the "passive" assigned to God, who strips the man and is never himself stripped? That is the first point.

source_text: Deinde si se homo ipse privat justitia, nonne hoc satis est ut sit justitia privatus? Quid opus est, ut postquam sese ipse privavit justitia, Deus eum privet justitia? oportet enim hanc privationem illa posteriorem esse, siquidem illa est violatio legis, haec illam violationem consequens poena. Praeterea, quaero, privatio justitiae originalis quatenus fuit in Adamo, aut est in nobis omnibus, qualis sit privatio? si est activa, habeo quod volo, est violatio legis, non autem poena lege denunciata. Si est passiva, non est violatio legis, non est peccatum, sed poena tantum. Id quod est negare peccatum originale. Denique, Docet-ne alicubi Scriptura Deum privasse Adamum justitia? Quomodo ergo ausus est Vir Doctus id asserere? Certe, qua ducor erga Deum reverentia, ferre non potest mea conscientia illam assertionem. Nam qui privat hominem justitia, facit eum injustum ejusque injustitiae causa est. Id quod vel suspicari de Deo mihi nefas esse videtur. Sed secundam affert Vir Doctus responsionem, qua tollit id quod dedit: eam audiamus.
english: Second: if the man has already stripped himself of righteousness, is that not enough for him to be without it? Why must God strip him again afterward? The divine stripping would have to come later than the self-stripping, if the latter is the law-breach and the former its following penalty. Third I ask what sort of privation original righteousness is, in Adam and in us. If active, I win: it is law-breaking, not a legally announced penalty. If only passive, it is neither law-breaking nor sin but bare penalty—and that denies original sin. Fourth: does any Scripture say God stripped Adam of righteousness? How then dare the learned man assert it? Reverence for God will not let my conscience bear that claim. Whoever strips a man of righteousness makes him unjust and causes his injustice—an idea I may not even entertain of God. But now he offers a second reply that retracts what he just gave; let us hear it.

source_text: GAR. 2. Si rem diligenter attendimus, patebit privationem activam justitiae, qua scil. homo amittit justitiam & ea seipsum spoliat, non esse formaliter idem cum violatione praecepti divini. Itaque verum quidem erit in sensu causali violationem divini praecepti esse justitiae privationem, quia scilicet ex violatione consequitur illa privatio; quo sensu dicitur dolor esse solutio continui, quia ad solutionem continui sequitur: sed in sensu formali non erit verum, ita scilicet ut reapse unum idemque sint, nec differant, nisi nominibus. PLAC. Ego vero existimo, privationem pro distinctione termini seu formae, cujus est privatio, distingui debere. Est autem justitia duplex, actualis nempe, & habitualis. Forma mali moralis, seu peccati collocari solet in privatione boni. Justitiae igitur actualis privatio est formaliter peccatum actuale; justitiae vero habitualis privatio est formaliter malum seu peccatum habituale. Nonne? Cum ergo actualis violatio legis formaliter opponatur justitiae actuali, hoc est, inobedientia obedientiae, necesse est ut actualis violatio legis sit formaliter actualis privatio justitiae, & cum habitualis violatio legis seu inobedientia formaliter opponatur habituali justitiae seu obedientiae, necesse est ut ipsa quoque sit formaliter privatio justitiae habitualis, atque adeo peccatum habituale. Sed contra disputat Vir Doctus tribus rationibus.
english: Garissoles' second reply. Attend carefully and active privation of righteousness—losing it and stripping oneself of it—is not formally identical with breaking the divine precept. Causally one may say precept-breaking is privation of righteousness, because the privation follows the breach (as pain is called a dissolving of continuity because it follows that dissolving). Formally they are not one thing under two names.

Placeus. I take privation to track the form of which it is the privation. Righteousness itself is twofold: actual and habitual. Moral evil, or sin, is usually formalized as privation of a good. So privation of actual righteousness is formally actual sin, and privation of habitual righteousness is formally habitual evil or sin. Is that not so? Actual law-breaking stands formally opposite actual righteousness—disobedience opposite obedience—so actual law-breaking is formally actual privation of righteousness. Likewise habitual disobedience stands formally opposite habitual righteousness, so it too is formally privation of habitual righteousness, that is, habitual sin. Against this the learned man brings three arguments.

source_text: GAR. Etenim 1. non unum idemque sunt, quorum unum idem homo eodem tempore velle potest, & alterum nolle. At ita habet in hac causa. Adamus enim de fructu interdicto comedens, volebat violare Dei praeceptum, sed nolebat justitiam suam & praerogativas amittere.
english: Garissoles' first reason. Things are not one and the same if a man can at once will the one and refuse the other. So here: Adam, eating the forbidden fruit, meant to break God's command, yet did not mean to lose his righteousness and privileges.

source_text: PLAC. Utraque propositio est falsa; Major quidem; potest enim unum idemque homo idem eodem tempore ob diversas rationes velle & nolle. Idque evenit frequenter: inde haesitatio, & deliberatio, & pugna nonnunquam inter cogitationes volitionesque nostras. Deinde est voluntas rectae rationi conformis, & est voluntas errans & rectae rationi repugnans: haec secum ipsa nonnunquam pugnat. Denique nemo vult malum qua malum formaliter, hoc est, quatenus est privatio boni. Itaque mirum videri non debet, si Adamus privationem justitiae formaliter non voluit. Ita enim peccatum suum voluisset sub ratione mali. Quod etiam in Minore ait, Adamum voluisse violare Dei praeceptum, materialiter tantum ut sic loquar, non formaliter, verum est. Voluit enim id quod erat violatio praecepti Dei, sed non sub ratione violationis praecepti divini, sed sub ratione magnae cujusdam bonitatis sibi falso apparentis. Quod si formaliter volebat violare Dei praeceptum, & tamen nolebat justitiam suam amittere, stultus erat, putans separari posse, quae separari nullo modo poterant.
english: Placeus. Both premises fail. On the major: one and the same person can, for different reasons, will and refuse the same thing at once—hence hesitation, deliberation, and the clash among our thoughts and choices. There is a will aligned with right reason and a will that errs against it; the erring will sometimes fights itself. No one formally wills evil as evil—as privation of a good—so it is no wonder Adam did not formally will the loss of righteousness; that would have been to will his sin under the aspect of evil.

What Garissoles says in the minor—that Adam willed to break the precept only materialiter, not formaliter—is right. Adam willed what was in fact a breach of God's command, but under the guise of some great apparent good, not under the aspect "breach of divine law." If he had formally meant to break the precept and yet refused to lose righteousness, he would have been a fool, imagining inseparable things could be parted.

source_text: GAR. 2. Ea non sunt unum & idem, quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquis violare legem, qui tamen propterea justitia sua habituali actu non privabitur, quod patet exemplo fidelium, qui subinde peccant, nec tamen privantur ea justitia, quam Deus spiritu suo in ipsorum cordibus operatus est.
english: Garissoles' second reason. Things that can really be separated are not one and the same. Someone may break the law and still not, in the act, lose habitual righteousness—as the faithful show, who sin from time to time yet keep the righteousness God works in their hearts by his Spirit.

source_text: PLAC. Conclusionem non expressit: haud enim ex duabus illis praemissis concludi potest id quod ei probandum incumbebat. Agitur enim non de omni violatione legis, sed de tali, nempe prima illa Adami, nec de qualibet privatione justitiae, sed de privatione justitiae qua praeditus erat ante lapsum Adamus. De hac enim violatione & privatione intelligenda est argumenti mei propositio minor. Aut igitur universalem esse oportebat Viri Docti Minorem, aut nominatim de illa privatione & violatione intelligi. Neutrum cum sit factum, nihil potest concludi mihi repugnans. Deinde simili argumento possent infinitae propositiones verissimae refelli, etiam ista, homo est animal. Nam ea non sunt unum & idem quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquid esse animal, nec tamen esse homo.
english: Placeus. He never states the conclusion; those two premises cannot yield what he needs to prove. The question is not every law-breaking, but Adam's first; not any loss of righteousness, but the loss of the righteousness Adam had before the fall. My minor is about that breach and that loss. Garissoles' minor must either be universal or name that case; neither done, nothing against me follows.
The same pattern would overturn endless true propositions—even "man is an animal." Things that can really be separated are not identical; something can be an animal and yet not a man.

source_text: Distinguo tamen ut supra justitiae privationem. Est enim privatio justitiae actualis & privatio justitiae habitualis: illa est violatio legis actualis, haec habitualis. Sed rursus distinguenda est justitia: accipi enim potest vel forensi significatione vel morali. Utraque rursus vel est legalis vel evangelica. Justitia forensis legalis, quia consistit in perfecta totius vitae conformitate cum lege, vel unica legis violatione amittitur. Una enim ad condemnationem sufficit. Evangelicae dispar est ratio: cum enim in remissione peccatorum consistat, palam est violationem legis non excludere remissionem peccati. Justitia vero morali sensu accepta opponitur, ut dixi, violationi legis, hoc est, injustitiae, actualis quidem actuali, habitualis vero habituali. Sed quaeritur an violatio actualis inducat necessario privationem justitiae habitualis? Distinctione opus est. Dispar enim est ratio habitus justitiae naturalis seu legalis, qualis ponitur esse in Adamo, & habitus justitiae supernaturalis seu evangelicae. Illa enim nec spem includit remissionis peccatorum, nec aliunde pendere videtur quam a facultate hominis naturali. Itaque violatione legis amittitur. Haec vero quia fidem ac spem remissionis peccatorum includit, & pendet ab alio principio quam humano, nempe a Spiritu regenerationis Sancto, & Decreto electionis, simplici legis violatione non excutitur. Est etiam violatio legis duplex: una est universalis a Deo ἀποστασία, seu mutatio finis ultimi, altera, particulare quodvis peccatum: Illa habitum justitiae delet, haec laedit quidem, at non destruit. Cum ergo justitia Adami legalis ac naturalis esset, ejusque peccatum universalis quaedam a Deo apostasia, seu finis ultimi mutatio, fieri non potuit, quin simul ac peccavit justitia privaretur, nec opus fuit, ut Deus judiciaria aliqua actione eum justitia privaret.
english: I still distinguish, as before, privation of righteousness: actual and habitual—actual law-breaking and habitual. Righteousness itself must be split again: forensic or moral; and each either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal righteousness is perfect lifelong conformity to the law, so a single breach loses it—one is enough for condemnation. Evangelical forensic righteousness rests on remission of sins, so breaking the law does not shut out forgiveness.

Moral righteousness stands opposite injustice—actual to actual, habitual to habitual. Does an actual breach necessarily strip habitual righteousness? Distinguish. Natural or legal habit (as in Adam) neither hopes for remission nor rests on anything but natural faculty, so law-breaking loses it. Supernatural or evangelical habit includes faith and hope of remission and hangs on the regenerating Spirit and the decree of election, so a mere breach does not shake it off.

Law-breaking itself is twofold: universal ἀποστασία from God—a change of the last end—or any particular sin. The first destroys the habit of righteousness; the second wounds it but does not wreck it. Adam's righteousness was legal and natural, and his sin a universal apostasy, a turn of the last end; so the moment he sinned he lost righteousness, and God needed no separate judicial act to strip him of it.

source_text: GAR. 3. Denique sicut actus illi, quibus habitus comparatur, non sunt ipsa habitus acquisitio, sed ad eos consequitur acquisitio: ita etiam actus, quibus excutitur habitus, non sunt ipsa habitus privatio, sed ad eos consequitur illa privatio. Frustra ergo jactat Vir Doctus in Thesibus suis de statu hom. Lapsi ante Grat. Th. 24. Nos hoc ipso justitia privari, quod legem transgredimur, & hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio introducta est in Adamum, ab eodem expulsam esse justitiam. Etenim si intelligit transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis justitiae, facile agnoscimus. Si putat transgressionem legis & privationem justitiae nihil inter se differre omnino, non probamus: quia transgressio legis est actio, privatio justitiae passio est: at pati & agere plusquam verbis differunt: Et Deus animas hominum creat justitia originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis praevaricatrices. Sic expulsio justitiae est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem justitiae: antecedens autem & consequens, nonnihil differunt inter se, ut opinor: Et Deus hominem concessis creatione donis spoliavit, quem tamen non corrupit.
english: Garissoles' third reason. Acts that build a habit are not themselves the acquiring of the habit—acquisition follows them. Likewise acts that shake a habit off are not themselves the privation—privation follows them. So Placeus boasts in vain in his Theses on fallen man before grace (Th. 24): that we lose righteousness by the very fact that we break the law, and that the change which brought corruption into Adam itself expelled righteousness from him.

If he means law-breaking is the meritorious cause of losing righteousness, we grant it. If he thinks law-breaking and privation of righteousness differ not at all, we refuse: breaking the law is an action; privation is a passion; acting and suffering differ more than in words. God creates souls without the ornament of original righteousness yet does not, by creating, make them law-breakers. Expulsion of righteousness precedes corruption; corruption follows expulsion—antecedent and consequent differ. God stripped man of creation's gifts yet did not corrupt him.

source_text: PLAC. Aberrat etiam haec responsio ab argumenti mei propositione minore. Cum enim dixi, privationem justitiae esse violationem conditionis seu praecepti, id ita accipi debuit, ut privatio justitiae actualis esse intelligeretur violatio actualis, & privatio justitiae habitualis, violatio habitualis. Sed videtur habituale peccatum Vir Doctus nullo fere loco habere. Itaque non frustra est quod me jactasse dicit in Thesibus: quo verbo, seu jactationem seu jactantiam significet, cur uteretur quam ei ansam praebuerim non possum videre. Divisi autem quae conjunxit, hocque dilemmate sum usus. Si justitia sumitur sensu forensi, nonne ea privamur hoc ipso quod legem transgredimur? In hoc dilemmatis membro quid reprehendat, aut reprehendi possit, non intelligo. Sequitur alterum; Si sensu morali: Annon hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio contraria justitiae in Adamum introducta est, ab eodem expulsa est justitia, haud aliter quam obtenebratione aeris expellitur lumen, aut frigesactione calor? In his quoque verbis meis quid reprehendit? Si intelligo transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis justitiae facile agnoscit. Hoc vero si intelligerem mecum ipse pugnarem, qui hoc, de quo agitur, argumentum affero, ut probem privationem justitiae originalis non esse poenam proprie dictam. Certe transgressio legis injustitia seu privatio justitiae est; justitia, inquam, actualis si est actio vel actionis omissio, habitualis vero si est habitus: transgredimur enim legem non solum actione, sed etiam habitu. Si puto transgressionem legis & privationem justitiae nihil inter se differre omnino, non probat. Ego vero nihil aliud volo, quam ut propositio mea vera sit, sive attributum & subjectum nihil omnino differant, sive differant nonnihil. Nam propositiones, homo est animal, homo est risibilis, verae sunt, quamvis subjectum & attributum plusquam nominibus differant. Sed quomodo probat differre? transgressio, inquit, legis est actio. Omnisne transgressio? non habitualis, ut opinor, nec ea actualis, quae in omissione actionis consistit. Sed pergat. Privatio justitiae passio est. At modo distinguebat privationem in activam & passivam. Est-ne igitur privatio activa passio? non sit veri simile. Passiva quoque, estne passio? at dicitur respectu Dei qui omnis passionis est expers. Certe privatio formaliter non est passio, sed reducitur ad praedicamentum formae seu termini cujus est negatio. Hoc docent omnes Logici. Passio non minus quam actio transit; Privatio vero permanet, etiam postquam actio & passio desierunt esse. Passio formaliter est ens reale, & per se est in praedicamento, privatio nec formaliter est ens sed negatio potius, nec in praedicamento nisi reductive. Mitto alias differentias inter passionem & privationem. Addo posita actione, cujus terminus sit accidens, poni necessario passionem; hancque ab illa non realiter differre, sed respectu tantum & ratione. Quod subjungit, Deus animas hominum creare justitiae originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis praevaricatrices, illud quale sit considerari oportet. Nam creat quidem animas justitia privatas, sed sic tamen, ut hujus privationis autor non sit, eam ipsae contrahant a corpore. Alioquin enim eas, si privaret justitia, faceret injustas. Nam inter justum & injustum, sanctum & pollutum in subjecto capaci nullum est medium. Quid porro est, quod addit, Sic expulsio justitiae est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem justitiae? Primo enim expulsio justitiae, praesupponit justitiam praeexistentem in subjecto unde expellitur. Non fuit autem originalis justitia nisi in solo Adamo. Ab eo igitur solo expulsa est. Deinde quis credat Deum ab homine justitiam expellere, ac propterea quod ab eo expulsa sit, ei irasci? Item Deum causam esse privationis justitiae, nec tamen esse causam corruptionis? Perinde enim est, ac si eum dicerem, qui tollit a corpore rectitudinem, non esse causam obliquitatis, aut qui tollit a corpore humano sanitatem, morbi causam non esse. Mihi quidem certe videtur nec corruptio moralis absque privatione justitiae, nec privatio justitiae absque corruptione morali consistere ullo modo, aut intelligi posse. Nam sive privative justitia & corruptio opponuntur, haec illius privatio est; sive contrarie, expellunt sese mutuo ex eodem subjecto capaci, & quidem immediate. Nullum enim medium concipi animo potest inter justitiam & injustitiam, virtutem & vitium, rectitudinem & obliquitatem &c. in subjecto capaci.
english: Placeus. This answer also misses my minor. When I said privation of righteousness is breach of the condition or precept, I meant actual privation as actual breach, habitual privation as habitual breach. Garissoles scarcely allows habitual sin a place. Calling my Theses "boasting" I cannot see what handle I gave him. I split what he joined and used this dilemma.

If righteousness is forensic, do we not lose it by the very fact of breaking the law? I see nothing to fault there. If moral: was righteousness not expelled from Adam by the very change that introduced the contrary corruption—as darkening drives out light, or cooling heat? If he takes me to mean law-breaking is only the meritorious cause of privation, he grants it; were that all I meant I would contradict myself, since I argue that privation of original righteousness is not punishment properly so called. Law-breaking is injustice—privation of righteousness—actual if act or omission, habitual if habit; we break the law by habit as well as by act.

He does not prove they differ "not at all." I only need my proposition true whether subject and attribute are identical or differ somewhat—as "man is an animal" and "man is risible" remain true though subject and attribute differ more than in names. "Law-breaking is an action"—every breach? Not habitual; nor actual omission. He says privation is a passion, yet had just split privation into active and passive. Is active privation a passion? Unlikely. Is "passive" a passion when said of God, who suffers nothing? Formally privation is not passion but reduces to the predicament of the form it negates—so the logicians. Passion passes with action; privation remains. Passion is a real being in a predicament; privation is rather a negation, in a predicament only reductively.

As for God creating souls bare of original righteousness without making them transgressors: he creates them without righteousness, yet is not author of that privation—they contract it from the body; else by stripping them he would make them unjust, and in a capable subject there is no middle between just and unjust. "Expulsion precedes corruption"? Expulsion presupposes righteousness already in the subject; original righteousness was only in Adam, so only from him was it expelled. Who believes God expels righteousness and then is angry because it is gone—or causes the privation yet not the corruption? That is like saying who takes straightness from a body does not cause crookedness, or who takes health does not cause disease. Moral corruption and privation of righteousness cannot stand or be thought apart. Whether they oppose privatively or contrarily, they drive each other out of the same capable subject at once; there is no middle between justice and injustice, virtue and vice, straight and crooked, in a capable subject.

source_text: Noli mihi objicere peccatum esse interdum poenam peccati. Primum enim non est poena quatenus peccatum, nisi velis duas species mali oppositas inter se confundere, sublato inter malum poenae & culpae discrimine. Privatio autem justitiae in nobis, qua talis, formaliter peccatum est; repugnat enim legi. Deinde id non est accipiendum de poena proprie & stricte accepta, qualem lex comminatur & justitia necessario exigit ut sibi satisfiat. Quis enim credat justitiam exigere ut justitia violetur? satisfieri justitiae eo quo justitia laeditur? solvi poenae debitum eo, quo debitum illud augetur? Adjungi praecepto, ne violetur, comminationem poenae sitae in violatione praecepti? pergo igitur.
english: Do not tell me that sin is sometimes the punishment of sin. First, sin as sin is not punishment—unless you mean to smash together two opposite kinds of evil and erase the line between penalty and guilt. Privation of righteousness in us, as such, is formally sin; it clashes with the law.

Second, that claim is not about punishment properly and strictly so called—the kind the law threatens and justice must have satisfied. Who believes justice demands that justice be broken? that justice is paid by wounding justice? that the penalty-debt is settled by making the debt larger? that a threat whose penalty is the very breach of the precept should be tacked onto the precept "do not break it"? I go on.

source_text: Quarta ratio, poena proprie dicta sive mors quam lex comminabatur sequi debuit quaestionem ac judicium Dei de violatione illius legis. Sed privatio justitiae sive mors spiritualis quaestionem ac judicium Dei de violatione legis sequuta non est, sed antecessit: non fuit igitur poena proprie dicta, sive mors quam lex comminabatur.
english: Fourth proof. Proper punishment—the death the law named—has to come after God has examined and judged the breach. Loss of righteousness, spiritual death, did not wait for that examination and judgment; it arrived first. Therefore it was neither proper punishment nor the death the law was threatening.

source_text: Quinta denique ratio, (caeteras enim differre, & in alium locum conferre satius erit.) Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus (ut tu asseris) prout Deus minatus fuerat, Mortuus est. Id autem mihi falsum videtur. Nam primo, Tu, opinor, fateris Adamo condonatum fuisse primum illud peccatum, numerando alioquin inter damnatos: non igitur, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus est. Pugnant enim haec duo, condonari peccatum & puniri secundum legem. Deinde, Tu per mortem denunciatam comminatione tam mortem corporis & aeternam intelligis, quam spiritualem illam. Pertinebat igitur aeque ad veritatem comminationis & justitiam, ut, quo die legem violavit, eodem tam corporea & aeterna morte, quam spirituali moreretur. Tamen eodem die neutram passus est, aeternam autem nunquam subiit, aut subibit. Cur non potuit Adamo mortis spiritualis aeque ac aeternae poena condonari? aut saltem differri?
english: Fifth proof (I put the rest off for another place). If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, then—on your view—Adam died just as God had threatened. That looks false to me. First, you yourself, I take it, grant that Adam's first sin was forgiven; otherwise he would be counted among the damned. So he did not die just as God had threatened. Forgiveness of sin and punishment according to the law cannot both stand.

Second, by the death named in the threat you mean bodily death and eternal death as well as spiritual. Truth and justice in the threat would then require that on the very day he broke the law he die bodily, eternally, and spiritually. Yet that day he suffered neither bodily nor eternal death, and eternal death he never underwent and never will. Why could spiritual death's penalty not be forgiven Adam as eternal death's was—or at least deferred?

source_text: His accedat Scripturae Testimonium: colligens enim summam annorum vitae Adami Gen. v. vers. 5. non contenta iis verbis, quibus in similibus computationibus solis usa est constantissime, interferuit haec duo, וַיְחִי, proculdubio nec frustra, nec temere: quo tamen pertineant non video, nisi ut innuatur, Adamum, ut ferebat divina comminatio, non fuisse mortuum, sed vixisse; quod aliunde quam a Dei gratia, & Domini nostri Jesu Christi satisfactione proficisci non potuit. Hoc ipsum etiam ex eo potest intelligi, quod sententia Adamo lata in paradiso non fuit definitiva, sed quasi interlocutoria, dans spatium homini ad resipiscendum, dilato post mortem extremo judicio, ac interim conditionem hominis definiens, mediam quodammodo inter damnatum & absolutum. Hinc factum est, ut, neque Deus hominem pronunciaverit maledictum, quemadmodum serpentem, sed terram duntaxat. Et quamvis morti corporeae eum addixerit sententia, tamen circumlocutione usus sit, nec mortem eam appellare voluerit, ne videretur pertinere ad Comminationis legis executionem. Fuit igitur judicium illud, non extremum (hoc enim Adamo post mortem subeundum fuit juxta illud Apostoli, statutum est hominibus ut semel moriantur, postea vero judicium Heb. 9.) sed praemissum extremo in aliud tempus dilato. Vide sis Thesium mearum de lapsu Adami ultimam.
english: Add Scripture's witness. When Genesis 5:5 totals Adam's years, it is not content with the words it always uses alone in like reckonings; it inserts these two, וַיְחִי—surely neither for nothing nor by chance. I see no point for them except to hint that Adam, as the divine threat would have it, had not died but had lived—and that life could come only from God's grace and our Lord Jesus Christ's satisfaction.

The same follows from the paradise sentence: it was not definitive but, as it were, interlocutory—giving the man room to repent, deferring the last judgment until after death, and meanwhile setting his state somehow between the damned and the acquitted. Hence God did not call the man cursed as he did the serpent, but only the ground. And though the sentence bound him to bodily death, it spoke by circumlocution and would not name it "death," lest it look like executing the Law's threat. So that judgment was not the last (Adam must face that after death, per the Apostle: it is appointed for men to die once, and after that judgment—Heb. 9) but a preliminary to the last, deferred to another time. See the last of my Theses on Adam's fall.

source_text:
Si igitur Deus pro summa sua misericordia & sapientia comminationis illius executionem distulit, ac suspendit ex alio judicio post separationem animae a corpore futuro, fatendum est Adamum non fuisse, prout ferebat legis comminatio, Mortuum. Itaque comminationem illam de spirituali morte posita in privatione justitiae non esse intelligendam, quam ego arbitror ipsa morte aeterna deterius malum esse.

GAR. Additur & tertia ratio. Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus, prout Deus comminatus erat, mortuus fuerit, quod falsum; cum inter damnatos non sit computandus. Item, cum mors illa aeternam, corporalem, & spiritualem complectatur, qui nunquam sensit aeternam, nec statim sensit temporalem, quomodo spiritualem, nempe privationem justitiae, statim incurrisset? Respond. 1. Qui mortuus est morte sita in privatione justitiae, si in ea perseveret, usque ad finem, inter damnatos computandus est. At non ita factum Adamo, qui fide in semen benedictum ex illa morte spirituali in vitam spiritualem excitatus est, ut fit omnibus electis, quos mortuos in peccatis placet Deo vivificare in Christo, Ephes. 2.
english: If then God in supreme mercy and wisdom deferred executing that threat, hanging it on another judgment after soul and body part, we must grant Adam was not Dead as the law's threat required. So the threat of spiritual death as privation of righteousness is not to be read as I take that threat—which I judge a worse evil than eternal death itself.

Garissoles. A "third" reason is added. If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, he would have died as God threatened—which is false, since he is not to be counted among the damned. And since that death covers eternal, bodily, and spiritual: he who never felt eternal death, nor at once felt temporal, how did he at once incur spiritual death—privation of righteousness? Reply 1. Whoever dies the death of privation of righteousness and stays in it to the end is counted among the damned. Not so Adam: by faith in the blessed seed he was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, as with all the elect whom God is pleased to make alive in Christ when dead in sins (Eph. 2).

source_text: PLAC. Cur hanc rationem, cum sit quinta, tertiam vocet, causam nullam video, nisi quia, cum duas praeterierit, secundam & quartam, videri tamen noluit ullam praetermisisse. Quatuor etiam rationibus minorem hujus argumenti quinti confirmaveram: ex quibus solas priores duas sibi objicit, sed ita contractas, praesertim primam, ut vix eam agnoscam. Adhibet autem responsiones duas, quibus argumentum firmare potius videtur, quam infirmare. Priore rationem reddit, cur Adamus non fuerit damnatus. Concedit igitur, (quae minoris argumenti mei confirmatio erat) eum non fuisse damnatum. Sic enim se habebat argumentum meum; Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus est. Atqui Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus non est. Ergo Lex non comminabatur Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae. Quid respondet Vir Doctus ad Majorem? Num eam negat? Num distinguit? Num ei limitationem adhibet? Nihil prorsus respondet. Eam igitur concedit. Ita videtur. Potest tamen limitari: cum enim praeter illam privationem, etiam corporis & aeternam mortem lex minaretur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem partim punitus fuisset, partim non fuisset: Punitus fuisset illa privatione seu morte spirituali, non fuisset punitus morte corporis & aeterna. Sed haec limitatio argumento nihil nocet. Punitus enim saltem fuisset poena aliqua proprie dicta, seu judiciaria quam Lex comminabatur, & quidem poena maxima. Id autem est falsum. Fecit enim ei Deus gratiam peccati. Non punitur autem cui peccatum remittitur, cui peccatum non imputatur, qui justificatus est a peccato. Nam si partim puniretur, partim non puniretur, etiam ei partim peccatum remitteretur, partim non remitteretur, & partim justificaretur, partim non justificaretur; imperfectaque esset justificatio, id quod Evangelicorum nemo dixerit. Cum tale sit argumentum meum, vides, lector, hanc priorem Viri Docti responsionem illius neque majorem, neque minorem labefactare. Pergat igitur.
english: Placeus. Why call this the third reason when it is the fifth? I see no cause except that, having skipped the second and fourth, he still did not want to seem to have skipped any. I had backed this fifth argument's minor with four reasons; he takes up only the first two, so compressed—especially the first—that I scarcely know them. His two replies seem to shore the argument up more than tear it down.

The first explains why Adam was not damned—and so grants what confirmed my minor: he was not damned. My argument ran: If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, Adam was punished as the law threatened. But he was not. Therefore the Law did not threaten him with that death. What does Garissoles say to the major? Deny? Distinguish? Limit? Nothing at all—so he concedes it.

One might limit: besides that privation the law also threatened bodily and eternal death, so Adam would have been partly punished (by spiritual death) and partly not (by bodily and eternal). The limit does not hurt the argument. He would still have been hit by some punishment properly so called—judicial, and the greatest—which the Law threatened. That is false. God granted him grace for the sin. The one whose sin is remitted, not imputed, who is justified from sin, is not punished. Partial punishment would mean partial remission and partial justification—an imperfect justification no evangelical would own. So, reader, this first reply shakes neither major nor minor. Let him go on.

source_text: GAR. 2. Nihil in eo mirum quod Adamus & statim a peccato privationem justitiae incurrit, & nec aeterna morte damnatus est, nec temporalem statim sensit. In spiritualem statim incurrit, ita volente Deo, ne si statim in eum non incurrisset ulla species mortis, videri posset Adamo verior Satanae promissio, non moriemini omnino, quam Dei comminatio, morte moriemini; & in peccato consenescens Adamus de seria poenitentia & conversione ad Deum forte non cogitasset: sed pupugit eum praesentis poenae sensus, ut ad Deum resipiscendo rediret, quem rebellando deseruerat. Mortem vero temporalem non statim incurrit, ut poenitendi tempus ipsi concederetur, quod nullum est post mortem. Hanc poenam eodem quo peccavit die Adamus luisset, nisi visum fuisset Deo ob futuram Christi Satisfactionem, spatium dare generi humano ad agendam poenitentiam, inquit Vir Doctus Disput. de lapsu Adami Thes. ultima. Denique aeternam omnino non incurrit, quia erat inter electos Dei, in quos infernus nihil habet juris. Apocal.
english: Garissoles. 2. No wonder Adam at once lost righteousness by the sin, and yet was not damned to eternal death, nor felt bodily death at once. He fell into spiritual death at once—God willing it—lest, if no kind of death had struck him at once, Satan's promise (you will not die at all) should look truer to Adam than God's threat (you will die the death); and lest Adam, growing old in sin, should never think of serious repentance and return to God. The sting of present punishment pricked him so that he might repent and come back to the God he had left by rebellion.

Bodily death he did not meet at once, so that time to repent might be given him—there is none after death. He would have paid that penalty the very day he sinned, had God not, for Christ's coming Satisfaction, chosen to give the human race space for repentance (so the Learned Man says in his Disputation on Adam's fall, last thesis). Eternal death he never met at all, because he was among God's elect, over whom hell has no claim. (Apocalypse.)

source_text: PLAC. Haec posterior responsio ad secundam Minoris argumenti mei confirmationem spectare videtur: Sed primo eam non attingit; Deinde sese ipsa contradictione implicat; Denique se praebet ridiculam. Sic enim se habebat illa confirmatio, ut eius vim explicem, Cui, quo die peccavit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna, is non est eo die, sicuti Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus. Atqui Adamo, quo die peccavit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna. Ergo Adamus non est eo die, sicuti Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus.
english: Placeus. This later reply seems aimed at the second support of my minor. First it never touches that support. Then it contradicts itself. Finally it turns silly.

The support ran thus: Whoever, on the day he sinned, was not hit with bodily death or eternal death, did not die that day as God had threatened. But Adam, the day he sinned, was not hit with bodily death or eternal death. Therefore Adam did not die that day as God had threatened.

source_text: Nihil potest responderi, nisi, ei quidem inflictam non fuisse mortem corporis & aeternam, sed tamen inflictam fuisse mortem animae positam in privatione justitiae. Sed contra sic insto. Si inflicta ei fuit mors animae, ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Sed non ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Ergo ei inflicta mors illa non fuit. Major negari non potest. Minorem probo. Si ideo ei inflicta fuit mors animae, quia id exigebat comminatio, etiam ei inflictae fuerunt mors corporis & aeterna, quia hoc non minus exigebat comminatio. Attamen hae mortes non sunt ei inflictae. Ergo mors animae non est ideo ei inflicta, quia id exigebat comminatio. De minore nulla lis esse potest. Major, quanquam aperte vera est, tamen eo confirmatur, quod non minus mortem corporis & aeternam Deus comminatus fuerat quam spiritualem. Haec igitur si Dei veritas, & justitia exigebant ut eo die Adamo infligeretur, eadem, veritas & justitia, non minus exigebant, ut illae etiam mortes infligerentur eadem die; par, uti vides, ratio est. Quod huic argumentationi dissolvendae accommodatum sit, nihil animadverto in responsione Viri Docti.
english: The only way out is to say: bodily and eternal death were not laid on him, yet the soul's death—privation of righteousness—was. I press against that. If the soul's death was laid on him, it was laid on him because the threat required it. But it was not laid on him because the threat required it. So that death was not laid on him.

The major stands. For the minor: if the soul's death was laid on him because the threat required it, then bodily and eternal death were laid on him too, for the threat required those no less. Yet those deaths were not laid on him. So the soul's death was not laid on him because the threat required it. The minor is beyond dispute. The major, already plain, is confirmed because God had threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual. If God's truth and justice required the spiritual death that day, the same truth and justice required those other deaths the same day—the reason is the same. I see nothing in the Learned Man's reply that dissolves this.

source_text: Ea autem, quod secundum erat eius peccatum, sese contradictione involvit. Nam qui potuisset Adamus retinens justitiam originalem, quae sine dubio injustitiae seu peccato opponitur, consenescere in peccato, manere a Deo aversus, Dei desertor, Deo rebellis? Quid enim erat justitia illa, nisi conversio cordis ad Deum, obedientia habitualis Dei mandatis, constans voluntas obediendi Deo, jusque illi suum tribuendi, qua, hoc ipso quod ipsi inerat, justus erat Adamus? Quis ergo futurum fuisse credat, ut Adamus, nisi amitteret justitiam, consenesceret in peccato? Contra enim consensisset in justitia, si quidem justitiam non amisisset. Se quoque ridiculam praebet haec responsio, cum fingit ablatam fuisse Adamo justitiam, ut ad Deum resipiscendo rediret. Tantum enim abest, ut mors spiritualis medium sit ad resipiscentiam, & conversionem ad Deum, ut eam homini reddat impossibilem, eumque a Deo longissime abducat. Ridiculum etiam mihi videtur, quod dicitur, pupugisse Adamum praesentis illius poenae sensum.
english: His second point wraps itself in contradiction. How could Adam, still keeping original righteousness—which is the opposite of unrighteousness and sin—grow old in sin, stay turned from God, desert God, rebel against God? What was that righteousness but a heart turned to God, habitual obedience to his commands, a steady will to obey him and give him his due—the very thing that made Adam righteous while it was in him? Who believes Adam would have grown old in sin unless he had lost righteousness? He would have grown old in righteousness if he had kept it.

The reply also turns silly when it pretends righteousness was stripped from Adam so he might repent and return to God. Spiritual death is so far from being a path to repentance and conversion that it makes them impossible and drives the man farthest from God. And it is silly to say the 'sense' of that present penalty pricked Adam.

source_text: Habitus enim non sunt qualitates sensibiles, neque sentiuntur, aut intelliguntur a nobis, nisi quatenus ex antecedentibus aut consequentibus actibus inesse deprehenduntur. Adde quod mors spiritualis, quantum ad veram pietatem attinet, hominem sensu privat, & facultate bene agendi, eumque ad omne bonum opus ineptum, ad omne malum pronum, aversum a Deo, conversum autem ad carnem & ea quae Deus odit, efficit.
english: Habits are not sensible qualities. We neither feel nor understand them except as we infer them from acts that go before or follow. Add this: spiritual death, for true piety, strips a man of sense and of the power to do well. It makes him unfit for every good work, ready for every evil, turned from God, and turned to the flesh and to what God hates.

source_text: Temperare mihi non possum quin sextam rationem superioribus adjungam, ductam primum a phrasi illa morte morieris: Nam nullus quod sciam locus extat in scriptura, ubi phrasis illa morte mori de figurata illa morte sit accipienda, quae nihil aliud est quam absentia sanctitatis in anima. Deinde ab ipso nomine mortis, quod in vetere Testamento mihi non occurrit eo sensu, Immo ne in Novo quidem absolute, & sine additamento, nisi forte Luc. ix. 60. sine ut mortui sepeliant suos mortuos: quo tamen loco non videtur Dominus ad privationem originalis justitiae communem omnibus respexisse, sed ad incredulitatem & contumaciam. Cum enim qui non credit jam sit condemnatus Ioh. 3. 18. & super eum ira Dei maneat. Ioh. 3. 36. nihil prohibet incredulum mortuum appellari. Fac tamen eum ad privationem illam respexisse, solemne ei est vocabula transferre a propria & communiter usitata significatione ad spiritualem & metaphoricam lucis Evangelicae ad tempus tegendae causa, in quo eum imitari non debuerunt Apostoli. Iam quis credat primam illam dei legem & comminationem conceptam verbis usitatissimis morte morieris, intelligendam esse sensu prorsus inusitato, & quidem ita ut idem vocabulum semel positum, semel intelligendum, accipiatur simul & proprie, & metaphorice. Possum te obruere aliis argumentis, sed non sunt omnia simul ac semel effundenda.
english: I cannot help adding a sixth reason to the ones above, drawn first from the phrase 'you shall die the death.' I know no place in Scripture where 'to die the death' is taken of that figured death which is only absence of holiness in the soul. Next, from the name 'death' itself: I do not find that sense in the Old Testament, and not even in the New used absolutely and without addition—unless perhaps Luke 9:60, 'let the dead bury their dead,' where the Lord seems to mean unbelief and stubbornness, not the privation of original righteousness common to all. For whoever does not believe is already condemned (John 3:18), and God's wrath remains on him (John 3:36)—so an unbeliever may well be called dead.

Grant that he meant that privation: it is his way to shift words from their proper, common sense to a spiritual, metaphorical one, to veil the Gospel light for a time—and the Apostles should not have copied him there. Who then believes God's first law and threat, set in the most ordinary words 'you shall die the death,' must be read in a sense wholly unused—and so that the same word, used once and to be taken once, is taken both properly and metaphorically at once? I could bury you with further arguments, but not everything must be poured out at once.

source_text: GAR. Ultimo sic argumentatur. Mors spiritualis est mors metaphorice dicta; mors corporalis proprie. Quis autem existimet in lege, quae debuit verbis usitatissimis concipi, vocabulum unum, idemque debere accipi simul & proprie & metaphorice? praesertim cum morte mori figurato sensu, nescirem accipi, nisi forte Luc. IX. 60.
english: GAR. Finally he argues thus. Spiritual death is death said metaphorically; bodily death, properly. But who would think that in a law that had to be framed in the most ordinary words, one and the same term should be taken both properly and metaphorically at once—especially when I would not know 'to die the death' in a figured sense except perhaps at Luke 9:60?

source_text: PLAC. Vides, ut meam istam rationem contrahit, ut magna sui parte truncat, ut mihi tribuit, id quod non dixi, morte mori usurpari Luc. Ix. 60. Pergat tamen.
english: PLAC. See how he shrinks that reason of mine, cuts away a large part of it, and credits me with what I never said—that 'to die the death' is used at Luke 9:60. Still, let him go on.

source_text: GAR. Resp. Agnoscit Vir doctus, mortis nomine, tum mortem corporalem, tum etiam aeternum inferorum cruciatum intelligi, ut audivimus. Quid ergo responsurus est, si quis hoc argumentum ipsi reponat; vocem eandem in lege, quae debeat verbis usitatis concipi, non posse simul proprie & metaphorice sumi: cruciatum autem inferorum esse mortem metaphorice dictam, cum sola corporalis sit mors proprie dicta: ergo non posse his verbis intelligi cruciatum illum.
english: GAR. Reply. The learned man grants that 'death' covers both bodily death and the eternal torment of hell, as we have heard. What then will he say if someone turns his own argument back on him: the same word in a law that should use ordinary language cannot be taken properly and metaphorically together; hell's torment is death only metaphorically, since only bodily death is death properly so called; therefore those words cannot mean that torment.

source_text: PLAC. Ego vero respondebo, cum de foro Dei agitur nullam magis proprie mortem dici quam aeternam: a qua si corporalis sejungitur, ne mors quidem amplius vocari debet ipso Christo autore: Eam enim non comminatur lex, nisi quatenus est jactura omnium huius vitae bonorum. Jactura autem non est, cum in eorum locum succedunt meliora. Adde quod mors aeterna corporalem includit, id est, huius vitae privationem, ut illam: comminari lex non potuerit, quin istam simul comminaretur.
english: PLAC. I answer: before God's court no death is more properly called death than eternal death. If you split bodily death off from it, even that no longer deserves the name 'death,' by Christ's own teaching. The law threatens eternal death only as the loss of all this life's goods—and that is no loss when better goods take their place. Add that eternal death includes the bodily—the loss of this life—so the law could not threaten the one without also threatening the other.

source_text: GAR. 2. Cum Deus hic omnem mortem comminatus sit, qua dignum erat peccatum Adae, quidni dicamus & corporalem & spiritualem & aeternam fuisse comminatam, cum is omnibus subjacere mereatur peccator? PLAC. Omnis mors, qua dignum est peccatum, est mors diversa a peccato. Mors autem spiritualis est peccatum, & meretur mortem. GAR. 3. Nec vero Scripturis inusitatum est mortis nomine, mortem spiritualem designare, cum contrarium pateat, non modo ex Luc. 9. 60. Sed etiam ex frequentibus testimoniis, quorum etiam nonnulla jam produximus. PLAC. Non dixi inusitatum esse Scripturis nomen mortis pro morte spirituali: Dixi tantum inusitatum esse Scripturae veteris Testamenti, dixi toti Scripturae inusitatam esse phrasim, morte morieris eo sensu. Id ad meam istam rationem attineat. Jam laudaverat, nam ex Ezech. 3. 18. & ex Hos. 13. 1. sed frustra; nam ut ne ei opponam interpretes neutrum locum de morte spirituali accipientes, reclamat ipsa res. Agitur enim in illis locis de morte, quae non est omnium hominum communis, sed de morte in quam incurrunt quidam ob sua quaedam peccata actualia, cum mors spiritualis omnium sit hominum, & quidem ab ipso eorum ortu, antecedens omnia ipsorum actualia peccata. Itaque non possunt loca illa de spirituali morte, in privatione justitiae originalis sita, accipi.
english: GAR. 2. Since God here threatened every death Adam's sin deserved, why not say he threatened bodily, spiritual, and eternal death, when the sinner deserves to lie under them all?
PLAC. Every death that sin deserves is a death other than sin. Spiritual death is itself sin, and it merits death.
GAR. 3. Nor is it unusual in Scripture to call spiritual death by the name 'death'; the opposite is clear not only from Luke 9:60 but from many other texts we have already cited.

PLAC. I did not say Scripture never uses 'death' for spiritual death. I said only that that sense is unused in the Old Testament, and that the phrase 'you shall die the death' in that sense is unused in Scripture as a whole. That is what my reason needs. He had already appealed to Ezek. 3:18 and Hos. 13:1—but in vain. Even without opposing interpreters who take neither place of spiritual death, the subject itself objects: those texts treat a death not common to all, but a death some incur for particular actual sins, whereas spiritual death belongs to all from birth and precedes every actual sin. So those places cannot mean spiritual death as the privation of original righteousness.

source_text: GAR. 4. Verbis usitatis, id est, vulgo notis leges concipi debere fatemur. Sed quis dicat verba metaphorica & impropria non esse usitata? Imo metaphoris nihil communius, etiam in legibus sanciendis, quae saepe una voce multa complectuntur, eaque diversissima, ut ad unius vocabuli proprietatem redigi non possint, sicuti patet in praeceptis Decalogi. PLAC. Dixine verba metaphorica, & impropria non esse usitata? Dixi tantum nomen mortis eo sensu metaphorico & improprio, quo significat mortem spiritualem, seu privationem justitiae originalis, non esse usitatum in vetere Testamento. Non negavi quin usurpentur interdum metaphorae in legibus, tantum negavi eas usurpari, quae sunt eo tempore, quo leges feruntur, inusitatae: negavi etiam eandem vocem in eadem lege semel usurpatam, simul & proprie & metaphorice intelligi debere. Tum enim demum accipi debet metaphorice, cum aliquid obest, quominus accipi possit aut debeat proprie. Neque propterea duplicem sensum Scripturae nego, literalem & mysticum: ille enim est verborum, hic potius rerum. In praeceptis Decalogi nullam vocem video, quae simul & proprie & improprie, seu metaphorice debeat exponi.
english: GAR. 4. We grant that laws should be framed in ordinary, commonly known words. But who says metaphorical or improper words are not ordinary? Metaphors are nowhere more common than in framing laws, which often pack many and very different things into one word that cannot be reduced to a single proper sense—as the Decalogue's precepts show.

PLAC. Did I say metaphorical and improper words are unused? I said only that 'death' in the metaphorical, improper sense that means spiritual death—or the privation of original righteousness—is unused in the Old Testament. I never denied that laws sometimes use metaphors; I denied using metaphors that were unusual when the laws were made, and I denied that the same word, used once in the same law, must be read both properly and metaphorically at once. Metaphor comes in only when something blocks taking the word properly. That does not make me deny Scripture's double sense, literal and mystical: the first belongs to the words, the second rather to the things. In the Decalogue I see no word that must be read both properly and improperly—or metaphorically—together.

source_text: GAR. Denique pari argumento utuntur Pontificii, ut probent illa verba, hoc est corpus meum, non esse intelligenda figurate, quia pactum, sacramentum, lex, requirunt propriam non figuratam locutionem: ita enim Bellarminus & Costerus. Nostri respondentes negant, ut videre est apud Chamierum lib. 10. de Eucharist. cap. 15. n. 60. 61.
english: GAR. Finally the Papists use a like argument to prove that the words 'this is my body' must not be taken figuratively, because a covenant, a sacrament, and a law require proper—not figurative—speech: so Bellarmine and Coster. Our writers deny it in reply, as you may see in Chamier, book 10 on the Eucharist, chapter 15, §§60–61.

source_text: PLAC. Si dicerent Pontificii in verbis hoc est corpus meum, non esse metaphoram inusitatam, aut non esse eandem vocem simul proprie & non proprie seu improprie accipiendam, quia id non ferat pactum, Sacramentum, lex, recte procederet comparatio, neque nostros haberent repugnantes. Nunc cum ab illis verbis, omnique pacto, sacramento, & lege omnem excludant metaphoram, etiam admodum tritam & perspicuam, quid est illis mecum commune? Certe eos refutavi Exam. rat. pro & contra Sacr. Missae part. I. c. xiv. pag. 429. & seqq. Negari autem non potest, quin verbis morte morieris, proprie dicta mors designata fuerit. Sic meas defendi rationes. Suas etiam quasdam habet Vir Doctus, quibus probet, mortem, quam Deus illa lege comminatus est, non tantum esse mortem corporis, verum etiam mortem animae, id est, amissionem justitiae originalis, & imaginis Dei privationem. Eas expendi par est.
english: PLAC. If the Papists said that in 'this is my body' there is no unusual metaphor, or that the same word is not to be taken both properly and improperly at once—because a covenant, sacrament, or law would not bear that—the comparison would run straight, and they would not find our men opposing them. But when they shut every metaphor out of those words and out of every covenant, sacrament, and law—even a worn, clear metaphor—what do they share with me? I answered them in my Examination of reasons for and against the Mass sacrifice, part I, chapter xiv, p. 429ff. It cannot be denied that 'you shall die the death' named death properly so called. So I defended my reasons. The learned man also has reasons of his own to prove that the death God threatened by that law is not only bodily death but also death of the soul—that is, loss of original righteousness and privation of God's image. Those reasons ought to be weighed.

source_text: GAR. Rationem triplicem producimus. Primum enim. Non alia mala & damna rebellione sua homo incurrit, quam quae interminatus fuerat ei Deus sua legis sanctione; quem enim ab inobedientia & praevaricatione legis absterrere voluit, quidni praecipitia ei posuisset ob oculos, in quae erat suae legis divinae violatione deturbandus? Atqui homo, sua obsequii denegatione, non mortem modo corporalem, & calamitates externas sibi accersivit, verum & omissionem spiritualium donorum, & facultatum omnium perversionem, & damnationis aeternae reatum incurrit. Omnia ergo Deus sua illa mortis declaratione comminatus fuerat.
english: GAR. We bring a threefold reason. First: man incurs by his rebellion no other evils and harms than those God had threatened by the sanction of His law. For if God meant to scare him from disobedience and law-breaking, why would He not have set before his eyes the precipices into which violation of the divine law would cast him? Yet by refusing obedience man drew on himself not only bodily death and outward calamities, but also the loss of spiritual gifts, the perversion of every faculty, and guilt of eternal damnation. Therefore God had threatened all of that by His declaration of death.

source_text: PL. Distinguo mala. Alia enim sunt culpae, alia poenae. Illa Deus lege sua vetuerat, non comminatus fuerat: haec comminatus fuerat, non autem vetuerat. Est autem mors spiritualis seu privatio justitiae originalis malum culpae, non poenae proprie dictae. Negatur igitur Major, si de culpae malis intelligitur. Quanquam ne de malis quidem poenae intellecta universaliter vera est. Distingui enim debent mala poenae in ea quae sunt poenae, ut loquuntur, satisfactoriae, & ea quae se habent aliquomodo ut carceris poenae & molestiae, vel ut castigationes paternae. Illas solas lex comminabatur. Incurrit autem in has homo per peccatum suum, quia propter Christi satisfactionem datum est ei ad resipiscendum spatium, & tractatur a Deo, ut solet a patre filius puer.
english: PL. I distinguish evils. Some are of fault, others of penalty. God had forbidden the former by His law; He had not threatened them. He had threatened the latter; He had not forbidden them. Spiritual death—or privation of original righteousness—is an evil of fault, not a penalty properly so called. So the major is denied if it means evils of fault. And even of penalty-evils it is not universally true. Penalty-evils must be split into those that are, as they say, satisfactory penalties, and those that stand somehow as prison pains and troubles, or as a father's chastisements. The law threatened only the former. Man falls into the latter by his sin because, for Christ's satisfaction, space was given him to repent, and God treats him as a father treats a boy.

source_text: GAR. 2. Adamus in integritate perseverans, bonorum & corporalium, & spiritualium continuatione & augmento donandus erat: Ergo & ab ea integritate deficiens, ut malis subiaceret, & corporalibus, & spiritualibus, consentaneum erat: quidni ergo Deus ea significata voluerit mortis nomine? PLAC. Atqui perseverantia in integritate & continuatio integritatis idem sunt. Integritas autem originalis & justitia originalis quid differunt? Erat igitur donandus continuatione, non justitiae originalis (haec enim continuatio exigebatur ut conditio) sed aliorum omnium bonorum. Porro integritas opponitur corruptioni immediate: deficere ab integritate est corrumpi, amittere integritatem est acquirere corruptionem. Confundit ergo Vir doctus conditionem promissionis cum re promissa: nec verum est argumenti ejus antecedens, nisi de bonis intelligatur physicis, seu ab ipsa integritate seu justitia diversis.
english: GAR. 2. Adam, if he had persevered in integrity, was to be given continuance and increase of bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore, falling from that integrity, it was fitting he should lie under bodily and spiritual evils: why then should God not have meant those by the name of death?

PLAC. But perseverance in integrity and continuance of integrity are the same thing. And how do original integrity and original righteousness differ? So he was to be given continuance—not of original righteousness (for that continuance was required as the condition), but of all other goods. Integrity is opposed immediately to corruption: to fall from integrity is to be corrupted; to lose integrity is to gain corruption. So the learned man confounds the condition of the promise with the thing promised; and his antecedent is true only of physical goods, or goods other than integrity or righteousness itself.

source_text: GAR. 3. Nulla ratio dici potest, quare non mortis nomen in tota sua latitudine hoc loco sumatur; atqui mortis nomen in Scripturis non ad corpus modo, sed & ad animam, & spiritualia referri patet ex frequentibus Scripturae testimoniis. Vide Ezech. 3. 18. Os. 13. 1. Matth. 8. 22. Luc. 9. 60. & 15. 24. Ephes. 2. 1. 1. Tim. 5. 6. Apoc. 3. 1. &c. PLAC. Ratio est in promptu, quia mors spiritualis est peccatum, non autem proprie loquendo peccati poena. Comminatur autem Lex non peccatum, sed proprie dictam duntaxat peccati poenam. Quod autem ait, non deesse auctoritates gravium virorum, nec desunt etiam mihi non minus gravium virorum auctoritates, & jam supra Helveticam laudavi confessionem Art. 8. Sed quid opus est humanis pugnare testimoniis, ubi rationes adsunt illis multo validiores? Caeterum vides quid hinc sequatur: nam si privatio justitiae non est poena lege denunciata, certe poena proprie dicta non est. Quare non est adscribenda justitiae vindici nobis peccatum illud actuale Adami imputantis.
english: GAR. 3. No reason can be given why 'death' should not be taken here in its full breadth; and Scripture plainly refers the name of death not only to the body but also to the soul and to spiritual things—see Ezekiel 3:18; Hosea 13:1; Matthew 8:22; Luke 9:60 and 15:24; Ephesians 2:1; 1 Timothy 5:6; Revelation 3:1, and so on.

PLAC. The reason is ready: spiritual death is sin, not—properly speaking—the penalty of sin. The Law threatens not sin, but only the penalty of sin properly so called. As for authorities of weighty men not being wanting—authorities of men no less weighty are not wanting to me either, and I already cited the Helvetic Confession, article 8. But why fight with human witnesses where far stronger reasons are at hand? For the rest, see what follows: if privation of righteousness is not a penalty the law denounced, it is certainly not a penalty properly so called. Therefore that actual sin of Adam is not to be ascribed to us by justice's avenger as He imputes it.

source_text: CAPUT V. Examen Cap. III. In quo disquiritur, Quid sit imputari vel non imputari peccatum. Capite tertio rursus constituis statum controversiae, eoque constituto iterum digrederis, ac tibi sumis illustrandum, quid sit imputare & imputari, ac primum verbum hebraeum, deinde verbum graecum expendis, laudatis in eum finem aliquot Scripturae locis: quorsum, aut quo consilio, nescio, nisi forte, ut tui tractatus molem augeres, ac tuorum argumentorum paucitatem tegeres: utilis quidem fortasse tua haec illustratio foret ad controversiam de justificatione: quoniam Scriptura eam solita est modo imputatione fidei & justitiae, modo non imputatione peccati describere: ad hanc vero, quae inter nos agitur, quaestionem quid valeat non video: Nullus enim extat in tota Scriptura locus, in quo peccatum Adami nobis imputari dicatur.
english: CAPUT V. Examination of Cap. III, in which it is asked what it is for sin to be imputed or not imputed. In the third chapter you again set the state of the controversy, and once that is set you digress again, and take it upon yourself to illustrate what it is to impute and to be imputed, and you weigh first the Hebrew word, then the Greek, citing some places of Scripture to that end—to what purpose, or with what design, I do not know, unless perhaps so that you might swell the bulk of your treatise and cover the scantiness of your arguments. Useful enough, perhaps, your illustration would be for the controversy on justification—since Scripture is wont to describe that now by the imputation of faith and righteousness, now by the non-imputation of sin—but for this question which is between us I do not see what it is worth: for there is no place in all of Scripture in which Adam's sin is said to be imputed to us.

source_text: Itaque non quaeritur inter nos, quo sensu Scriptura usurpet in hac quaestione verbum imputandi; nunquam enim usurpat, sed quo sensu in meis thesibus (quandoquidem tu eas refutare aggressus es) negaverim peccatum Adami nobis imputari, ut mea illa negatio, qualis sit, verane an falsa cognoscatur, ac vitetur παραλογισμός. Tandem concludis, peccatum imputari, cum attribuitur, consideratur, & pro peccato habetur & punitur ut peccatum; Ex opposito peccatum non imputari, cum non consideratur ut peccatum, sed tegitur, condonatur & remittitur. Quod certe non est accommodatum ad quaestionem nostram.
english: Therefore it is not asked between us in what sense Scripture employs the word 'to impute' in this question—for it never employs it—but in what sense in my theses (seeing that you have set out to refute them) I denied that Adam's sin is imputed to us, so that that negation of mine may be known whether true or false, and παραλογισμός avoided.
